ple randomization. hudimentary stratification was at-
tempted by Nagasue, Asahi, Osaka, and Jiji, while YKk em-
ployed the Fischer randomization tables to achieve ran-
domization rather than strict quota control. At the pres-
ent stage of development of Japanese public opinion re-
search, there is much. to be said in favor of strict ran-
domization as against quota allocation on a base of
faulty statistics. In default of accurate statistics et
the present time, it is impossible to estimete the magni-
tude of the sample error, but in very few cases does it
seem excessively high.
The second major technical improvement that may be
seen is the resort to direct personel interviewing rather
than to mail questionnaires or newspaper ballots. The
chances for representativeness and some degree of quota
control obviously are increased greatly by direct inter-
viewing, and a host of other technical controls which are
canonical in Americen pro:odure are made possible. All
of the major agencies employed direct interviewing.
The third major Improvement is specific to the field
of election studies, that is, in handling the problem of
turnout. A prediction based upon all of the ballots may
be accurate as to political preference, but it may not
predict accurately the trend of opinion of those who
ectually cast votes. American experience has shown that
there are differences in political direction between
voters and nonvoters. It is possible to demonstrate
clearly that increase in turnout favors one or the other
of the major political parties.4 In American voting be-
havior there is a definite selective factor, such that it
can be predicted within narrow margins of error that if
the total turnout is sich-and-such the nemocrets will in-
crease their majority, while if it falls below e certain
point the relative Republican position will be strength-

Three of the five Japanese agencies employed a

at considerable variance. The significance of these
facts will be discussed later in a point-for-point com-

YORON KAGAKU KYOKAI TOKYO MAYORALTY POLL
The Tokyo mayoralty elections were held on 5 April
1947. Several days before the elections, the Yoron Kagaku
Kyokai (Public Opinion Science Association) undertook to
attempt a prediction of the outcome. A screening question
was employed to determine probable nonvoting and thus to
be able to separate the probable voters from the probable
nonvoters.
In the Tokyo elections there were two principal can-
didates, one generally conservative and one socialist,
and a large number of minor candidates, all of them gen-
erally conservative.
Thus the results of the election
can be considered from the point of view of the distribu-
tion of votes among the candidates, or from the point of
view of general conservative vs socialist tendency. With
only one Socialist candidate, socialist opinion and sup-
port had only one place to go. But with about six gener-
ally conservative candidates, conservative opinion and
support could break up into various combinations, so that
even despite a conservative majority preference, the dis-
tribution of votes could possibly result in a Socialist
Party victory. The Jiji News Agency, which also conduct-

This study shows considerable technical skill in the
careful employment of small sampling. In addition to the
general success in prediction, other validity cen be dis-
covered internally in such items as the nonvoting predic-
tion. The estimate of nonvoting from a randomly-selected
number of the populsticn wes within seven percent of ac-
tual nonvoting.
This error is not too high in view of
the size of the sample and the uncertainty of voting in-
tention because of such factors as weather, degree of
structuring of opinion, intensity of politicel preference,
etc. YKk perhaps bent over backwards to make provision
for nonvoters, and may have listed more persons es poten-
tial nonvoters than it might otherwise have done.
At first glance the nonvoting figures seem to sug-
gest e phenomenon common in American elections: i.e., the
higher the nonvoting, the higher the proportionate con-

servative vote. In the current study, a nonvoting figure
of 50.5 percent was predicted. Coupled with it was a pre-
diction of a 54.1 percent vote for the conservative can-
didate. The actual results showed both a lower nonvoting
(i.e., a higher turnout) and a lower relative oonserva-
tive candidete majority, which would seem to suggest that
Socialist strength is greater with a higher turnout.
However, a closer examination of political dynamics,
by means of the consideration of pooled conservative-
Socielist votes, shows this not to be the case. That is,
the prediction, even with 50.5 percent nonvoting, turns
out to be just about the same as the actual results with
only 43.& percent nonvoting.
The conclusion from these figures would be that
there was no special selective fector or trend of politi-
cal preference among nonvoters as compared with voters.
Practically, it means that from the standpoint of survey
procedure, at least for the Tokyo area, a survey of pre-
ferences well could have been made without regard for the
problem of turnout, and an adequate prediction made.

There are several possible explanations of the error.
In the first place, it world appear that with the large
number of conservative candidates, voters had some diffi-

cielist minority, it would have been possible under the

win. This would account for the shift of 10 percent from

. Or in the third plece, a general populer trend of

It is important that in spite of the great differ-
ences between nonvoting predictions and the actual non-
voting results, the general trends of the predictions
were so close. This strongly suggests that there is no
politically selective factor operative in separating out
voters and nonvoters, whereas in general American experi-
ence, there is definitely a selective factor. This does
not seem to be the case at the present time in Tokyo, at
any rate.
Evidence from other parts of Japan is inconclusive,
but two further instances can be cited. The Asahi News-
paper Public Opinion Unit conducted gubernatorial elec-
tion prediction polls in several widely scattered prefec-
tures.
In two of the cases for which the results were
reported, Saitama and Kumamoto, Asahi was remarkably suc-
cessful in predicting the elections.
But in these two
cases no screening device whatsoever was employed to sep-
arate.voters and nonvoters.
If elections can be predicted both when a screening
device is used and when it is not used, the suggestion
seems strong that there is no important difference be-
tween voters and nonvoters in general political orienta-
tion.
However, these results are only tentative, end it
would be unsafe metiodologically to rely upon them. It

NAGASUE KYOTO MAYORALTY POLL
The Nagasue Public Opinion Research Institute in
Kyoto set out to predict the mayoralty elections of 5
April 1947. With the assistance of collaborators at Kyoto
Imperial University, and with careful regard for past ex-
periences, a very careful representative sample of 277
respondents was selected. Sixteen interviewers were sent
out with questions both as to political preference and
actuel intention to vote. On the basis of stated inten-
tiors of the respondents as well as the judgment of the
intorviewers, 96 ballots of persons who seemed unlikely
to vote were removed, and the prediction was mede on the
basis of the corrected tally of 18l probeble voters.
Thus, with good sample structure, a good questionnaire,
and alert interviewers, this device mede it possible to
predict with a degree of accuracy that would be consider-
ed quite respecteble in the United States.
It should be noted that contrary to usual Jepanese
practice up to the present time, Nagasue worked toward a
small and reliable sample, rather than a large and dif-
fuse one. The accurccy here is unusually high for small-
sample work. The results are shown in Table 20.
The most obvious technical improvements in the Naga-

AN EVALUATION OF SOME PRE-ELECTION STUDIES
The inconsistencies in comparative percentages between
party preference and candidate preference were, in some:
instances, striking. For instance, 44.4 percent of all
unemployed polled stated Socialist Party preference, yet
only 27.2 percent of all unemployed responding showed
Socialist candidate preference. Likewise, 16.7 percent
of all brainworkers polled stated Liberal Perty prefer-
ence, while.26:0 percent of all brainworkers. responding
showed Liberal candidate preference. However, these fig-
ures in themselves are misleading when it is understood
that of those unemployed and brainworkers responding to
the party preference question, only 30 percent of the
former and 56 percent of the latter responded to the can-
didate preference question.
These inconsistencies may be. better understood.
through further examination of question wording tech-
nique. When the human factors at work are taken into ec-
count, one may infer that the non-responding brainworkers
either were confused by much diverse publicity in elec-
tion cempaigns and could not decide which particular can-
didate to support, or they were still in the process of
evalueting, or they simply did not know the names of the
specific candidates, even though they had indicated a
party preference. At first glance the latter judgment
would not seem to be appropriate  for. "brain workers."
However, the fact is that the category of "brain workers"
here employed probably includes the entire gamet of non-
manual workers, including office workers, clerks, book-
keepers, professionals, and intellectuals. Therefore, it
is not surprising thet a certain percentage of so called
"brain workers" very likely did not name specific candi-
dates because of ignorance. In the case of the unemploy-
ed, the tables seem turned, the valid inference seeming
to be that a large percentage were ignorant of cendidate
names. However, this cetegory also includes brokers or.
black-marketeers who, living by their wits, probably would
be a sharper statum of this occupational breakdown, hesi-
tating to indicate candidate preference because of inde-
cision rather than ignorance.
These things cannot be shown clearly, however, by
means of such vague classifications as "brain workers"
and "unemployed." Furthermore, the entire occupational
breakdown suffered this same lack of specificity. This,
of course, was a result of the very small sample used, in

Question wording technique must be examined further

There is, however, another phase of question wording
technique to be considered. when measuring stetisticel
dete and drawing valid inferences therefrom. This is the
understandability of questions. and the presence or ab-
sence of psychological weighting. In opinion polling, the
questions must be uniform in level of stimulus and under-
stendeble as well. It is necessary to assure that direct
responses to direct questions are obtained, and that all
elements of ambiguity are eliminated. In a question such
as the one appeering on the Osaka poll, which reeds in
literal trenslation: "In the Osaka mayoralty elections do

politicel party, which one?" the question wording is am-
biguous because the term "neutrel" may include any one of
three or more categories. It may mean undecided as be-
tween the . political parties at the moment; it mey mean
that the respondent prefers an independent nonparty cen-
didate; and it may mean elso that the respondent is com-
pletely indifferent to the elections and will not vote.
Thus the use of the word "neutral" leaves the cetegory of
"neutral" answers unreliable and impossible of adequate
analysis. Alternate ques ion choices should have been
offered to independent, undecided, and indifferent re-
spondents, making it possible to understand the propor-
tions of eech category.

SUMMARY
It is possible to say at this point that the major
Japanese agencies have shown enormous improvement over
their work of last year. The improvements are princi-
pelly in respect to the employment of direct interviewing
methods, better sample randomization, and the considera-
tion by four of the five agencies analysed of the problem
of election turnout. In addition, we see in several cases
the beginnings of stratified sampling.
Meny shortcomings still remain, none of which, how-
ever, cennot be overcome in the reasonably neer future.
For example, the numbers of respondents  were in several
cases too small for significant analysis of voting dyna-
mics (YKK, Osaka, Nagasue).
Occupational breakdowns were not handled es they
might heve been.
For example, the Osaka Public Opinion
Research Institute used confusing and possibly overlap-
ping and nonexhaustive categories. In terms of known
voting dynamics, a category such as "ferm" would seem to
be insufficient, since the voting behavior of tenant-
farmers, owner-cultivators, and landowners differs redi-
cally.' The analysis of the rank order by occupetion in
Fumamoto and Saitama Prefectures by Asahi reveels this
clearly. Categories such as "brain workers" may include
clerks, writers, white-collar workers, etc.
However, on the balence, it would seem possible to
have more confidence in the results of work performed by
these egencies than would heve been justified a yeer ago.
Unless there sre redical departures in the present trends
of improvement, it should be possible to look to these
agencies for e good deal of informetion respecting public
opinion trends in Japan.
The polls all are agreed on the close relationship
between age and general perty affiliation, i.e., the
principle that the Socialist vote declines with ege and

=== Page 204 === (confidence 0.98)
.1
wishes to prejudge the review of the program. It therefore uses, as in
its first sentence, language of characterization to the effest that the
policy in SWNCC 302/2 "seens to be somewhat radical and of questionable
practicality". This language serves no useful purpose at this time and
tends to confuse an issue not yet decided. In effect, the Army is asking
us to concur on a few hours notice in a cable which prejudges important
issues now under review, without any evidence being introduced in support
of its judgment.
The Department of State has cooperated fully with the Army Department
in the earlier request to SCAP to delay action on the Ordinance and in
agreeing to review the whole program as set forth in FEC 230. The State
Departnent is preparing its own revision and your letter to Mr. Royall of
November 25 is the latest in a series of requests made by us for a statement
of Army objections to the paper in order that they may be considered in
this revision which may, for all we know, already have met many of the Army's
criticisms.
Apart from questions of basic approach, the effect of several of the
Army proposals for amendment of the Ordinances would be to weaken it to the
point of unworkability. It is hard to escape the impression that this is
what the Amy intends by the requirement that administration of its Ordi-
nance be peraissive rather than mandatory and that provision be made for
judicial review. The law could certeinly have been better drafted and it
is believed that the State Department's proposed amendments will improve
it. In any case, it is a necessary and proper part of the deconcentration
program. Its elesculation would heve serious adverse effects and would
indicate a reversal of basic policy.
The Army draft emphasizes the concept of "just compensation" and "fair
value" in such a way as again to prejudge one of the basic issues which we
have been endeavoring to discuss concretely with Army for some six weeks.
However, the question of compensation has almost no bearing on the Ordinance.
The type of reorganization contemplated is similar to the dissolution of
holding companies in the U. S. through distribution of portfolio securities,
the sale by cormorations of property unrelated to the main line of their
business, etc. Just as there is no provision in the United States Holding
Company Act, or Sherman Act, for "fair" compensation in connection with re-
organization, so also the question of compensation is largely irrelevant
with regard to the Japanese Ordinance. Anay concern with the question of
compensation may arise from a confusion between the purpose of the Ordinance
and that other aspect of the Zaibatsu program which relates to goverument
seizure and sale of the assets of Zaibatsu individuals. The program of
government seizure and sale went into effect in August 1946 pursuant to an
entirely different law and is now well advanced. The State Department is
prepared to consider further the question of compensation to these individuals
in the general review of the basic directive. To take up the problem out of
its main context by considering it in connection with the Ordinance may not
only prejudge the much larger issues but will also be misinterpreted by the
Japanese Government as placing a variety of unintended and unforeseen
limitations upon its power to reorganize Japanese enterprises.

=== Page 205 === (confidence 0.98)
The Army proposed the Agency administering the Ordinance not only to
determine that an enterprise was exerting a substantial influence on prices
but also to prove that the influence was "adverse". This provision would
place a burden on the Agency even greater in many cases than that required
by U. S. courts to be sustained under the Sherman Act. In the United
States price fixing is illegal per se whether benign or adverse. Bocause
of the virtual impossibility of comparing existing prices with prices which
would have been existing if a monopoly had not been present, this is the
only practical rule if enterprises of monopolistic characteristics are to
be defined as "excessive concentrations" under the terms of the Ordinance.
The Army draft would reguire that standards for determining excessive
concentrations be reviewed in Washington before promulgation. Even if the
necessary data and staff were present in Washington for such review its
effect could only be to emphasize to the Japanese responsible for admini-
stration there was considerable difference of opinion regarding the whole
progran between General MacArthur and Washington.
It is believed that the State Department draft goes as far as possible
in acceptin the Army suggestions and that it already oversteps the normal
prerogatives of SCAP and the Far Eastern Commission. Not the least serious
feature of the Army pronosals is that they would dictate General MacArthur's
action with a force and in a degree of detail which is in derogation of
international agreements whereby General LacArthur is Supreme Commander
for the Allied Powers and is to be instructed only by the issuance of
policy directives.
For the above reasons it is recommended that you forward to Mr. Royall
under the attached letter prepared for your signature, the State Department
draft cable, and the memorandum of comment, both of which are also attached.

AKAHATA

Full Translation.
Title: Aren't Repatriation Ships Coming Yet?
Subtitle: Japanese Detainees Waiting at Nahodka.
IINUMA, Tomoo (39), Tokyo correspondent of the HOKKAIDO
SHIMBUN, and late repatriate from Soviet Union blamed the
negligence of the Japanese Government for slowness in
repatriation work, on 28 November.
His statement was contrary to an answer given to ASAOKA,
Nobuo (Liberal), Upper House member who asked how the repatri-
ation of the Japanese countrymen in the Soviet Union is
coming along as winter sets in at the Upper House plenary
session. Welfare Ministry HITOTSUMATSU answered:
"The Government is doing its utmost to hasten the
repatriation of the Japanese people abroad and is fully pre-
pared to receive them."
IINUMA, who was repatriated from AJINIRIA (TN Trans-
literation) in Siberia in late October, made the following
statement in the anteroom of the Communist Party in the
Lower House:
"It is because of the negligence of the Japanese Govern-
ment that the repatriation from the Siberian area is not
going on smoothly. Repatriates from the Siberian area em-
bark at NAHODKA on Japanese ships to Maizuru. Japanese who
are to return to Japan are now being taken to NAHODKA intern-
ment camp from various places by the Soviet Union. When I
was at that place in September and October about 30,000
Japanese were concentrated there. However, only one
Japanese

=== Page 222 === (confidence 0.99)
Enclosure No.2,
Tokyo's Despatch No.1471,
December 22, 1947.
-2-
Japanese ship comes to NAHODKA once in three days, each
ship carrying only 2,O00 persons at a time. The KIZAN
MARU (6,900 tons) which I boarded took only 2,000 men on
board on account of food shortage, though it has accom-
modations for 5,O00 passengers. Therefore, there are
always about 20,000 to 30,000 Japanese countrymen eagerly
awaiting their return to homeland in the NAHODKA intern-
ment camp. This camp is actually made up of three camps.
Camp One is used for exchanging clothes; the second for
bathing and preparation for return; the third for
quarantine and customs inspections. The Japanese repatriates
must pass through these three camps before they can come
home. They are idling their time away without any work in
the first and second camps because transportation is not
available as stated before. Every camp is crowded with
homebound Japanese. Some of them are living in tents or in
the open. Some poor Japanese were even returned to the
hinterland working areas though they had finally reached
NAHODKA with much difficulties. I feel deep sympathy for
those Japanese who were obliged to go back to the hinter-
land again after seeing Japanese ships before their own eyes
because of food shortage on the ships.
"When I came back home I heard that the Soviet Union
has no intention of sending the Japanese back to Japan, but
this is absurd propaganda. However, I hear that the Japanese
Government has recently been trying a little harder to hasten
repatriation. However, repatriates' transportation is apt to
decrease considerably when winter sets in with its bad weather.
I feel very sorry that the Government did not endeavor to has-
ten repatriation much earlier. I was surprised at the bad
treatment on board the Japanese ship, which I boarded after
much difficulty. Half a military cup of rice-gruel and a tea-
cupful of miso (soy bean paste) soup was served as a meal.
Moreover, dried bread was served a meal once a day. I had a
hungry time for three days on board the ship, for I ate better
meals than I get now in Japan when I was a war prisoner in
Russia.
"The treatment at the time when we were interned was not
so good. The Soviet Union improved their treatment in work
and diet when we demanded it through collective bargaining
after we had democratized our military structure. I think
this was due to the power of democratic action and the Soviet
systen of adopting every measure if it is right."

OFFICE OF THE SUPREME

AG 000.73 (18 Sep 45)CI
MEMORANDUM FOR: IMPERIAL JAPANESE GOVERNMENT.
THROUGH:
Central Liaison Office, Tokyo.
SUBJECT:
Press Code for Japan.
1. News must adhere strictly to the truth.
2. Nothing shall be printed which might, directly or
by inference, disturb the public tranquility.
3. There shall be no false or destructive criticism
of the Allied Powers.
4. There shall be no destructive criticism of the
Allied Forces of Occupation and nothing which might invite
mistrust or resentment of those troops.
5. There shall be no mention or discussion of Allied
troops movements unless such movements have been officially
released.
6. News stories must be factually written and completely
devoid of editorial opinion.
7. News stories shall not be colored to conform with any
propaganda line.
8. Minor details of a news story must not be over-
emphasized to stress or develop any propaganda line.
9. No news story shall be distorted by the omission
of pertinent facts or details.
10. In the make-up of the newspaper no news story shall be
given undue prominence for the purpose of establishing or de-
veloping any propaganda line.
FOR THE SUPREME COMMANDER:
Harold Fair,
Lt Col, AGD,
Asst Adjutant General

Source: Daily Telegraph
December 23, 1947
JAPAN'S DOCILE APPRENTICESHIP IN DEMOCRACY
Malcolm Muggeridge
TOKYO
Defeat in Japan is less ostentatious than in
Germany, or even Italy. The Japanese appear to go
about their business with the same inscrutable deter-
mination as heretofore.
They give little indication of being under-nourished,
and though in towns like Tokyo and Yokohama there is stili
plenty of bomb damage to be seen, a great deal of clearing
up has been done and a large number of temporary buildings
have been erected.
Even in atom-bomb blasted Hiroshima the marks of
war are being rapidly obliterated, and the countryside
is for the most part quite unscarred. Its delicate
beauty remains, and the fields continue to be pain-
stakingly tended as though nothing had happened in the
world to disturb the even tenor of traditional ways.
The railway system was daliberately spared by American
bombing and is virtually intact.
THE EMFEROR IN HIS BOWLER HAT
Every day in Tokyo a little crowd collects in front
of Generai MacArthur's headquarters to watch the Supreme
Commander's arrivals and departures--C.I.s with their
inevitable cameras, Japanese who gaze with a mixture of
curiosity and awe at that remarkable man.
Nearby is the Imperial Palace where the Emperor
continues to reside, guarded by American and British
Commonwealth troops. His divinity has been at any rate
theoretically abolished, and on his occasional public
appearances he demonstrates his new status as a con-
stitutional monarch by a curious automatic raising and
lowering of his hat, usually a homburg but sometimes,
oddly, a bowler.
Further away, in ths former Japanese War Office,
a trial of Japanese war criminals is laboriously pro-
ceeding. It is now expected to drag on until well into
1948。
The two rows of accused display no omotion as they
listen attentively to the tale of their misdeeds. What-
ever regrets or contrition they may now feel finds no
expression in their outward demeanour. They might
,themselves be judges instead of the accused, so imper-
turbable is their bearing and so dispassionate are their
voices when they undergo cross-examination.
LEARNING/

=== Page 226 === (confidence 0.99)
UNCLASS IFIED
Page 2.
Encl. to Despatch 2956, December 23, 1947, from London
LEARNING THE BLESSINGS OF DEFEAT
If the first impression of post-war Japan is
that a military occupation has left the essential mould
of Japanese life intact, there prevails in General
MacArthur's headquarters an eager confidence that in
fact a social revolution drastically transforming the
country's economy, jurisprudence and administration has
already happened.
Whereas in the past representative covernment has
usually come to.pass as a result of a popular demand
for it, in post-war Japan the procedure has been reversed
and representative govarnment has been instituted in the
hope that thereby the Japanese may come to desire it.
It is as though King John should have drafted
Magna Carta on his own aocount with the intention of
encouraging his barons to demand his adherence to it.
A series of directives frcm General MacArthur's
headquarters have indicated to the Japanese the good
things which are in store for them in consequence of
their military defeat.
According to these airectives the blessings of
democracy and of an economy based on free competitive
enterprise which is sacured against monopolistic ten-
denciss have been conferred on them by S.C.A.P. (Supreme
Command Allied Powers), and it is for them to deserve
these benefits by effectively operating their new
constitution and by throwing themselves energetically
into the task of promoting Japan's sconomic recovery.
The new constitution, promulgated by the Emperor
a year ago, was draftsd by Japanese political leaders
in consultation with the Government Section of S.C.A.P.
for submission to the Diet, where it underwent consider-
able modification before it was finally approved. It
required and received the approval of General MacArthur
and of the Emperor.
By its terms the Emperor's powers have become those
of a constitutional monarch; the Diet, elected by
universal suffrage and a secret ballot, becomes "the
highest organ of State power and the sole law-making
organ of the State"; and the "whole judicial power is
vested in a Suprame Court empowered to dotermine the
constitutionality of any law, order, rogulation or
official act."
JUDGES MAY GET ORDER OF DISMISSAL
In its basic concepts the constitution is clearly
mod.elled on that of the United States. It would doubt-
less have astonished Jefferson and the other Founding
Fathers to kmow that their deliberations in Philadelphia
were before two centuries had run to find application in
remote Japan.
In one/

=== Page 227 === (confidence 0.99)
UNCLASSIFTED
Page 3.
Encl. to Despatch 2956, December 23, 1947, from London
In one respect the constitution follows English
rather than Amerioan usage. The Cabinet is directly
responsible to the legislature, consisting of an Upper
and a Lower House. Hereditary titles in the Upper House,
the House of Councillors, have been abolished.
A vote of no confidence involves a dissolution,
and Supreme Court judges, originally appointed by the
Cebinet, are subject to a "popular review" by means of
a referendum each ten years. If at this referendum a
majority of voters favour a particular judge's dismissal
he must be dismissed.
General MacArthur's officers tend to be more
enthusiastic and earnest than they are experienced
in administration and politics. But not even the most
enthusiastic and earnest among them would venture to
suggest that the mere promulgation of a democratic
constitution in itself transforms Japan from a highly
centralised authoritarian State into an authentic par-
liamentary democracy.
SUCCESS OF WOMEN'S FRANCHISE
They do, however, point to certain signs as being
encouraging. Female suffrage, they say, a startling
innovation for Japan, has been surprisingly successful
in the sense that in the two general elections so far
held women have voted in large numbers and apparently
on their own account.
Again, they point out, the size of the poll at
these elections--around 80 per cent in rural as well as
urban areas--indicated a remarkable degree of public
interest in the issues at stake. They regard the success
of the Social Democrats in the last election as authen-
tically rerlecting Japanese political sentiment at the
time, and consider that the present trend is to the
Right as represented by what is euphemisticelly called
the Liberal party.
In their view the constitution provides the means
whereby Japan may become a democracy provided the will
thereto exists. As already mentioned, the people are
being urged to he co-operative to that end.
In towns and villages posters and films and lectures
draw their attention to the advantages of their new con-
stitution and, as far as possible without direct inter-
feronce, Supreme Command Allied Powers steer the Diet
along the course it should follow in the liveliest
Capitol Hill tradition.
A visit to the Diet in session suggests that if
the zeal for democracy of some of the legislators remains
somewhat dubious, their aptitude for parliamentary pro-
cedure, incluuing a mastery or delaying tactics, is
unyuestioned. Their debates have often been turbulent
and their committee work is adroit.
KEEN/

=== Page 228 === (confidence 0.99)
UNCLASSIFIED
Page 4.
Encl. to Despatch 2956, December 23, 1947, from London
KEEN TO OBEY THEIR CONQUERORS
One of the 18 women members of the Lower House,
the House of Representatives, had occasion recently to
complain of fellow members arriving in the Chamber itself
in a state of intoxication, and some of the arguments
there seem to have taken a physical shape.
It is General MacArthur's legitimate boast that
the military occupation has proceeded almost without a
single act of violence. The Japanese have been and
remain astonishingly docile. Their sole ostensible
desire is to carry out their conquerors' wishes, some-
times even before these are formulated.
It is as though, having been defeated by the Amer-
icans, they have decided that American ways must be
advantageous, in the same way that in the past they
modelled their administration and army on Germany's,
their navy and banking system on England's.
Whether behind this outward docility secret pur-
poses are being entertained is a subject of heated
controvery among foreigners in Japan.
There are those who consider that the changes which
have beon introduced in Japan since the occupation began
have so far made little Impression on the traditional
manner of life.
WHEN THE GUIDING HAED WITHDRAWS
As they see it, the Japanese are quite capable of
bending the forms of Parllamentary democracy to their
own purposes, as they did the forms of Chinese civilisa-
tion when they decided to adopt them in the seventh
century A.D.
On the other hand, not unnaturally, those who
have been concerned in drarting and putting into effect
measures designed to democratise Japan are convinced
that, whataver may be the ultimate form or the Japanese
State derived from these measures, the Japanese people,
having tasted freedom for the first time in their his-
tory, will continuo to love it.
All that is certain now is that sooner or later
the controlling and guiaing hand of General MacArthur
will be withdrawn, and that then, with an impoverished
aconomy, in a turbulent world, and with only 125,000
police, mostly under municipal control, to secure law
and order, a Japanese Government responsible to an
elected Diet will have to face the future.

interest in urban areas seems to be considerably greater
than that in rural communities.

INTRODUCTION
A study of the indepancence of women's political atti-
tudes was conducted by tho Heinichi Newspaper Public Opin-
ion Room in April 1947. Three reas, Nakano Ward in Tokyo,
Ome City in Tokyo Prefecture, and Yuzurihara Village in
Yamanashi Prefecture, were selected in terms of differences
in urbanization and in cegree of familial control.
In each place, l0o ouples were interviewed on their
voting intentions towar the Liet elections. Two bnllot
forms were employed. Wives and husbands were interviewed
personally and se) rately on Ballot A. Ballot 3 was left
for each to fill out by nimself.
A comparison of the results of the two ballot forms
revealed that:
1. On the initial ballot, women were less decided on.
political matters than their husbands. Seventy-nine percert
of the men had made up their minds as to whom they were
voting for, but only 42 percent of the women had made a
decision.
2。
Political interest was highest in the city (69.5%),
lowest in the village (49%), and intermediate in the
town (63%).
3.
Rural women were least interested (29%), city women
most interested (53%), and town women intermediate (46%).
4. Disagreement between husbands and wives in voting in-
tention on the first ballot was nbout the same in city,town
and village.

=== Page 231 === (confidence 0.99)
2
MAINICHI STUDY OF WOMEN S POLITICAL ATTITUDES
5. Of those who disagreed on the first ballot, 76 percent
of rural women, 52 peroent of town women, and 36 percent of
city women respectively changed their minds in the direction
of their husbands' choice on the second ballot.
6. Only a amall percentage of men changed their minds in
the direction of their wives' choice on the second ballot.
From these data it seems possible to conclude that:
1.
Women are less interested in political matters than men.
2. Women still are influenced very considerably in their
political behavior by their husbunds' opinions, in spite of
their recently acquired rights of political franchise.
STUDY OF WOMEN'S POLIFICAL ATTITUDES
Under the new Constitution of Japan women have been
given equal rights with men. article 14 states: "All of
the people are equal under the law and there shall be no
discrimination in political, economic, or social relations
because of race, creed, sex, social status, or family origin."
In spite of the new emancipation accorded women, the
question arises as to how deeply the new laws penetrate the
traditional pattern of passivity and self-abnegation. Those
who oprose the granting of rights to women constantly have
put forth the argument that wo len do not use these rights
properly. They maintain that single women fall easy prey
to those who would buy their rights or coerce them, and
that married women do not use these rights independently,
but simply follow the dictates of their husbands. Because
of the feeling that women have little political importance,
some public opinion agencies in Japan deliberately under-
represented women in their snamples, stating that this would
not change the results of their surveys at all, since Jap-
anese women only reflect the attitudes and opinions of their
husbands or family heads.
What is the truth of these contentions? The answer to
this question obviously has reat political and social im-
portance. An approech to this question may be made by study-
ing the actual changes in the attitudes and the behavior of
the Japanese people hich have occurred since the-recent lib-
eration of Japanese women. One method is to examine the be-
havior of women in one of the areas of newly acquired rights.

=== Page 232 === (confidence 0.99)
:MAINICHI STUDY OF WOMEN'S POLITICAL ATTITUDES
The advent of the April 1947 Diet eleotione presented
the Mainichi Newspaper Public Opinion Unit with a valuable
opportunity to study the manner in which women exercise
their "eguality of franchise, " and to measure their polit-
ical interest.  This is a. very difficult thing to measure,
and several key factors had to be .examined and meaningful
controls set up.
In the present study, two factors known to have some
influence on the independence of women's political atti-
tudes were employed in the selection of a sample with which
to work. These were urban-rural differences and the strength
of familial controls. In the case of urban-rural differences
there are the highly conventionalized and relatively rigid
sooial patterns of the conservative, rural farm community
exerting strong and exacting pressures upon the individual,
especially the woman, as opposed to the loosely knit social
organization of communities consisting primarily of salaried
urban workers, where the old rigid controls are relaxed to
a great extent. Further ore, the rather great sociological
isolation of farm villages in Japan has tended to prevent
much interohange of ideas, whereas such intcrchange is al-
most inescapable in the crowded urban areas.1 That is, it
is reasonable to believe from general experience as well
as from the results of other public opinion and sociologi-
cal surveys, that country women are less interested in po-
litical matters than are city women, less educated, and
consequently less articulate and less likely to cast inde-
pendent baliots.
1.  The term "isolation" as used herein and clsewhere in
this report has the tcchnical meaning of separation
from centers of movements of thought, corresponding
to what the sociologist terms "mental isolation" and
the isolation of the "sacred society." Rural people
in Japan are not isolated from each other physically
or geographically, as they are in the United States,
but they are relatively isolated from the develop-
ment of new ideas and concepts. They live in a socio-
logically isolated environment, dominated by sacred
values, immobile, dominated by primary (face-to-face)
contacts, and by kin relntions, as distinguished from
the city people, who are characterized by high mobil-
ity, dominance of secular values, constant communica-
tion, dominance of seoondary contacts (non-face-to-
face), and dominanee of non-kin relations (employer-
employee, associations, government, unions, etc.)

=== Page 233 === (confidence 0.99)
4
MAINICHI STUDY OF WOMEN'S POLITICAL ATTITUDES
It is also reasonable to believe that women's politi-
cal independence will be affected by the extent to which
their position within the family is traditionally subeervi-
ent to the rule of the husband, who is termed in Japanese
shujin or dannasama meaning boss, lord and master, etc.
In Japan the extended family is more than just a general
term. It is a specific type of social organization. It is
called, technically, the dozoku? (same family) and consists
basically of a honke (main house) with its bunke (branch
houses). The main family units consist of the father and
mother and eldest son and his family. The bunke are branch
families usually set up for the younger sons, adopted sons,
grandsons, servants, loyal retainers of the family, etc.
When the main house has sufficient land and money, it will
build a house for one or more of the younger sons, depending
on the extent of their resourcos. Thus the bunke are set up.
In instances where the younger son or sons of the bunke fam-
ily can be provided with hous: and land, a magobunke (grand-
child branch family) is set v , either by the head of the
dozoku or head of the bunke. These relations of main house
to brench house then continue generation after generation
in a line of transmission through the eldest sons. All of
these branch families, whatever their nunber, are under
direct control of the main house, specifically the male
head of that house, to whom they owe many obligations and
duties, and from whom they receive many benefits. In many
cases, as for example, in the village studied in this survey,
the head of the main house is also the oyabun (boss), and
his branch houses his traditional kobun (retainers). Thus
the Jaranese extended family tends to be a working unit--
economic, social, and familial, under responsibility to its
main house, its units bounc together for mutual aid and
social action, co-operatin in their ritual life--through
many complex reciprocal relntionships.
With consideration of all the foregoing factors, there-
fore, the study of  men's political attitudes was set up
by mainichi Newspaper just prior to the April 1947 Diet elec-
tion. Three areas within 40 miles of each other, illustra-
ting significant differences in these diagnostic character-
istics, were chosen for the survey. They were: Nakano, an
urban ward of Tokyo with a hiyh percentage of salaried
workers and the modern "western" tyre of fa..ily structure;
2. Also known as jirui (land relative), maki (extended fam-

(one house). These ter..s are used in different parts
of the country.

Ome, a small country market town, part of Tokyo-Prefeaturm.

It seems significant that such. a large percentage of

around the dinner table with their husbands. The fact
that only 42 percent of all wives expressed political

interviewed were in agreement on the first ballot, whereas

understood at this point,however, that the conditions of
the study were not perfectly controlled. That is, influ-

GEN. MACARTHUR'S FAITH IN JAPAN'S REGENERATION
Source: Daily Telegraph
Malcolm Muggeridge
TOKYO
There is one name whicn will be forever associated
with the defeat of Japan and the subsequent military
occupation of the country, and that is, of course, Gen.
Douglas MacArthur.
He has shaped and executed occupation policy. As
Mr. Byrnes once frankly aámitted to Senator Brewster
in the course of a session of the Senate War Investi-
gation Committee, Washington has had little hand in
the Supreme Commander's conduct of Japanese affairs.
His pronouncements are rarely, if ever "cleared" with
the State Department. He goes his own way. In Tokyo
he is supreme.
Gen. MacArthur was kind anough to find time for a
talk with me. He received me in his office, seated with
his back to the window, smoking an exceptionally large
pipe. He looks younger than his 67 years, bright oyed,
scarcely grey at all, though with his hair somewhat
thinning in front.
His voice is resonant, and readily becomes fervid.
He talks impersonally rather than intimately. As he
gets into his subject the flow of words gains momentum
until it is difficult,probably impossible, to stem it.
He is well versed in british affairs. Like most
Americans he has a profound admiration for Mr. Churchill,
with whom, though he has never met him personally, he
naturally had much to do during the war.
REPUDLTCANSI CHOL.E?
Inevitably, such a man in such a position is a
subject of controversy.
There are those who complain or his theatricality,
and allege that he is surrounded by orficers who are
so anxious to please him that they only tell him what
they know he wants to hear. Others consider him the
greatest living American, and compare the order which
prevails, at any rate superficially, in Japan with the
strife and confusion elsewhere.
He is being freely mentioned as a possible choice
for the Republican Presidential nomination next June.
The General himself, despite repeated attempts to
extract from him a statement of his position, has so
far serupulously refrained from any but equivocal
comment.
On this/

=== Page 242 === (confidence 0.99)
UNCLASSIFIED
Page 2.
Fncl. to Despatch 2990, December 30, 1947, from London
On this subject, unlike most others, he is
prepared to listen but not to pronounce himself. The
fact that he listens suggests that the White House is
not beyond his consideration; the fact that he will
not pronounce himself suggests that he has still an
open mind on the subject.
Those who know him best believe that if he were
offered the nomination he would feel in duty bound
to accept it, and that with his now almcst mythical
reputation among Americans he would prove a formidable
candidate.
OCCUPATION POLICY
Even Gen. MacArthur's severest detractors all
admit that he is without question a great soldier.
Whether history judges him likewise to have been a
great administrator will depend on how his work in
Japan turns out.
On that it is too early yet to form a final opinion.
The General himself is firmly, even passionately, of
the opinion that the Japanese after centuries of slavery
have come to appreciate their new pclitical freedom,
and that whatever may hapnen suosequently they will not
be persuaded or coerced into letting it go.
He sees the occupation troops as having brought
to Japan, both oy precept and example, the essentials
of democracy and Christianity, the one embodying
politically and the other spiritually the sanctity of
the indiviaual.
In this way, he considers, through his agency a
revolution unparalleled in history has been brought
about which will infallibly result in the rogeneration
of the Japanese people.
There is no question of the General talking like
this just ror efrect. He believes what he says pro-
roundly and utterly. His officers have made it the
basisof the whole occupation policy of S.C.A.P. (Supreme
Conmand Allied Powers), and post-war Japanese political
leaders have been quick, whether sincerely or not, to
echo the Supreme Commander's sentiments.
THE PURGE
As part of this process of regenerating Japan it
was necessary to ensure that those Japanese who had led
the country into authoritarian ways, and finally into
war, should be deprived of the possibility of future
leadership, and to break up the concentration of economic
power in the hands of a few families, the so-called
Zaibatsu.
The former/

The former task was undertaken by means of a purge
aimed in Gen. MacArthur's words, at the "removal from
public office of undesirable leaders." This is, of
course, quite apart from the relatively few actual war
criminals who have been, or are in process of being,
tried on specific charges.
Unlike the German purge, Gen. MacArthur's is
specifically not punitive, and involves neither im-
prisonment nor coniiscation of property. So far about
200,O00 Japanese have been affected, and it is con-
sidered unlikely that other than occasional individual
cases will crop up in the future. The purge is con-
sidered now to have been virtually completed.
An obvious criticism of it is that though it may
achieve the exclusion from public office of those
identified with the pre-occupation regime in Japan in
that it leaves them with thsir property and social standing
intact, they are still in a position to influence, if
not clandestinely to direct, Japanese Covernment policy.
CHANGE IR TEMPO
Closely related to the purge is Gen. MacArthur's
poliey of "dissolving exoassive concentrations of
aconomic power into as many non-related units as possible."
To achieve this it was proposed to offer for sale
to the oneral public the immense industrial and aff-
iliated holdinrs of families like the Mitsui, reimbursing
them with non-transferable Government stock. In the
present inrlationary rinancial situation in Japan such a
progranne had littla chance of success, and the original
directive (Fac 23o) settinr it frorth has recently been
witndrawn after having been submitted to tho consideration
of the Far Eastern Commission in Washington on ay lz
last.
The obvious deduetion from its withdrawal is that
it has now been decided to procoed move cautiously, and
to
rebuila Jupan's oconomy to a greater extent than was
at first orvisaged on its existing foundations.
It is not only in regard to P30 230 uhat there has
lately been a change, ii not in policy in Japan, at any
rate in the tempo oi its execution.
Some three months ago Gen. MacArthur was taling
about the essential tasks of the occupation having been
completed. It looked then as though a peace conference
would be called before this year was out, and that a
speedy withdrawal of occupation forces was envisaged.
Now, in consequence of the attitude of China as
well as of Russia, tho prospoct of a peace treaty has
receded/

receded, and there is every indication that the occupation

orthern Japan large airfields are being rapidly con-

Two factors in particular have caused this changed

is the marked worsening of Russian-American relations,

Though the Wedemeyer Report on China has never been

A FAR EAST BASTION
In these circumstances the United States Government
has come to feel, with the undoubted concurrence of Gen.
MacArthur, that Japan will have to provide a necessary
bastion against Russian expansion in the Far East.
Such a policy would not necessarily involve an
inuefinite protraction of the military occupation of
Japan, which is oven now little more than a token occupa-
tion, with only 40, 000 American troops, some 10, 000
Dominions troops, ana 2,000 R.A.F. personnel.
These last are to be withdrawn early next year,
and it is anticipated that the Dominions forces will be
further reduced, perhaps down to 4, 000.
A permanent holding rorce of the size the United
States Congress would be likely to sanction would in
itself corstituts no security against invasior, say, from
Korea, where the prosent American position is militarily.
quite untenable.
At the same time, assuming, as must be assumed that
Chinese Communist, and therefore Russian, influence may
well before long extend as far as the Yullow River, and
that the United States Government is unable or unwilling
to sustain the Chiang Eai-shek regime, a demilitarised
Japan with for armed forces only 125,O00 civil police
wonld have little chance of standing alone.
NEW MONROE DOCTRINE
What is intended, therefore, if and when the present
occupation comes to an end, is the application to Japan
of something like the Monroe Doctrine whereby any attack
on that country would automatically constitute an act of
war against the United States.
This/

This might not prevent Japan from being invaded,

NEW AND OLD JAPAN
The passage of the economic decentrali-
zation Bill through the Japanese Diet
marks an important stage in the achieve-
ment of GeNerAL MacArthur's plans for
freeing the economic as well as the poli-
tical structure of Japanese society from
the grip of reactionary elements. The
Bill is intended to break the power con-
centrated in the hands of the Zaibatsu.
As a message from our Tokvo Correspon-
dent shows, it was opposed from widely
differing motives by several Japanese
political groups who resisted it with as
much strength as they have dared to show
against any measure pressed upon the
Cabinet by the Supreme Allied Command.
An unexpected complication was caused
by the leakage in Washington of the
confidential policy document known as
F.E.C. 230 upon which the Bill was based.
That document suggested that the break-
up of great industrial combines might be
followed by the sale of their constituent
enterprises to trade unions, among other
possible recipients, and this started a
scare in the United States that GENERAL
MAcARTHUR was aiming at the socializa-
tion of Japanese industry and playing into
the hands of the small Communist Party
now firmly entrenched in certain Japanese
trade unions.
This was a complete nisrepresentation
of the policy of the SUPREME ALLIED COM-
MANDER—F.E.C. 230 was, in fact, prepared
by the State Department, which has no
sympathy with Communists—but the
hubbub in Washington, which led to the
temporary withdrawal of F.E.C. 230,
caused GEnerAL MAcArTHUr to order
the Bill to be held up in the committee
stage of the Japanese House of Council-
lors until he had received further instruc-
tions. Moreover, the opposition of
Japanese big business interests, as well as
of the political parties, was greatly
encouraged. Fortunately the Government
of the United States realized the import-
ance of the issues at stake, and before the
end of the first parliamentary session held
under the new Japanese constitution
GENERAL MacArTHUR received official
authorization to proceed with the Bill with
insignificant amendments. It has now
passed into law.
The political and economic measures, of
Which GENErAL MACARTHUR is the prin-
cipal author, are heartily disliked by the
classes accustomed to monopolize power
in Japan. Much evidence has recently
como to light showing that they are wait-
ing patiently for a chance of regaining
their old authority. A "top secret"
document clandestinely obtained from the
Japanese Foreign Ministry and published in
the United States clearly reveals the plans
of the governing clusses for making light
of any restrictions upon Japanese sove-
reignty imposed by the peace treaty.
GENERAL. Tovo's obatinate defence of
Crimes Tribunal as simple national self-

=== Page 249 === (confidence 0.99)
throw democratic institutions when the
allied occupation eads Now they will
ind themselves much handicapped by lack
of financial support, and the economic life
of the country will be freed from the
stranglehold of monopolies. Although th
Japanese Government may be expected to
pursue its usual tactics of overt obedience
and covert obstruction, it will be poweriess
to prevent the allied liquidation commis-
sion froni destroying the influence of one
of the main forces now striving to restore
the domination of "Old Japan." The
result may be a lasting change in the struc-
ture of Japanese economy.
All this is particularly important in view
of the growing disposition of the allies to
make a definitive peace with Japan. As the
Canberra conference showed the nations
of the Commonwealth agree with the
United States that the interests of the
allies, as well as of Japan herself, will be
best served by bringing the allied occupa-
tion to an end as soon as possible. Now
that commercial intercourse between
Japan and the outside world, including the
sterling area, has begun again the indefinite
continuation (f allied supervision in its

help economic recovery. The progressive
elements which the new democratic insti-
tutions are bringing into prominenc: in
Japan will suffer in popularity if they are
indefinitely identified in the eyes of the

occupation forces.
This does not mean that reaction will-
be aliowed a free hand when peace is

GeNERAL MaCARTHUr is known to en-
dorse-contemplates a dual procedure for

would bind the Japanese Government to
accept in perpetuity not only the general
provisions for the restraint of future
aggression laid down at Potsdam but also
the specific measures of political and
economic reform introduced in the course
of the allied occupation. Thus the main-
tenance of the democratic framework now
set up will be among the specific obliga-
tions of the Japanese Government.
Secondly, there will have to be some allied
machinery for supervising the fulfilment
of these cbligations for at least a genera-
tion. This machinery could most conveni-
ently be provided by the Ambassadors of
the eleven nations represented on the Far
Eastern Commission. The Commission's
secretariat might be transferred to Japan
as the instrument of the new allied control.
The duration of the system beyond the
initial period of two or three decades
would depend entirely upon the progress
made by the Japanese people towards real
democracy and a peaceful outlook. No
Japanese Government should exercise un-
restricted control over national affairs
so long as there is any prospect of the
old reactionary force regaining influence.
A peace settlement upon these lines
should have the support of all the allies,
but the allies are not agreed on the pro
cedure to be adopted in making the peace.
The Soviet Government still insists that
the first steps should be taken by the
Foreign Ministers' Council, while the
countries of the Commonwealth and the
United States prefer a conference of all
the nations concerned. Certainly recent
experience in Lóndon does not suggest

WITH THE EMPEROR IN TIE RUINS OF HIROSHIMA
Malcolm Muggeridge
HIROSHIMA (delayed)
When American bombers began to go over Tokyo they
deliberately refrained from attacking the Imperial Palace.
The consequence was that at the time of Japan's defeat
tho Emperor's residence stood intact in the midst of a
largely ruined canital.
Its pleasant gardens and shaay groves were unscarred
by the war which had just erded so disastrously for Japan.
Tho Emperor himself and his household could await the
conoreror's cominr without physical discomfort, whatever
agonies of spirit they may have suffered.
This represented, of course, a deliberate policy,
decided on by the Allies before Japan's surrender, of
main taining the monarchy and thereby preventing the total
administrative breakdown which was otherwise to be expected.
As long as the mperor remained, it was felt, orders
would continue to be obeyed. Discipline in the armed
forces and civil Service would bo maintained, and it would
be posslolo to rufashion the Juoanese State without
totally disruptin it.
MILLTON ALLIED LTVES JERE SAVED
No aspact of Gen. MacArthur's poliey has been more
criticised than the decision to keep the Emperor on his
throne, thouch with greatly reduced status and with his
powers those or a constitulional Sovereign.
As the rormer supreme head of the Japanese State,
in whose name Japan propared ror and ruthlessly pursued
a policy of military acression, it is argued, his place
is in the dock with the other war criminals rather than
in the palace of his ancestors. In allotting responsi-
bility for war crimes, how is it possible to avoid
implicating the Emperor on whose behalf, at any rate
ostensibly, they were committed?
When I asked Gen. Robertson, the energetic and
exceedingly competent Commander-in-Chief of the British
Commonwealth Occupation Forces in Japan, what he thought
about the decision to treet with the Emperor, thereby
recognising/

=== Page 254 === (confidence 0.97)
UNCLASSIFIED
Page 2.
recognising him as spokesman of the Japanese people, he
said that probably as many as a million Allied lives
were at stake.
At the time of the armistice, he pointed out, there
were 46 Japanese divisions actually in Japan to defend
the country against invasion, and subsequent survoys
had shown beyond a shadow of doubt that to achieve landings
in accordance with Allied invasion plans would have proved
appallingly costly in life.
SYMBOL THE JAPANESE LISCONSTRIED
It was only because the order to cease fire came
from the mperor that it was obeyed and that Allied
forces were able to land in Japan practically without
bloodshed.
Thus on two counts, both weighty, the decision to
maintain the Emperor on his throne can be justified--
that otherwise there would have been heavy Allied losses
in effecting a landin in Japan and a total administrative
breakdown after one had been effected.
On the other hand, it must be admitted that it is
difficult to discredit a regime when its titular head,
its very symbol in the eyes of the Japanese population,
continues to be accorded recognition by the occupying
forces.
Moreover, the Japanese are prone, somewhat ominously,
to claim that, since they did not surrender unconditionally,
they cannot he said to have been defeated in battle.
Their surrender, they say, was contingent on the
Allies accoptin: the Mmperor as head and mouthpiece of
the nation, whe could not be held responsible for the deeds
of mere qovernments, ever thouch their authority was
derived from him. It is not dirficult to see how sueh a
concept could easily lond itself to the kind of myth which
provided tho mystique for lerman rearmament and revenge
arter the 1914-18 war.
ACOLADELG TES OYAL TOURTST
If the Emporor still remains on his throne his
situation is vastly different from what it was before
Gen. MacArthur came to Tokyo. Prom being a od upon whom
his subjects were not even permitted under pain or death
to cast their eyes he has become a man whose voice and
featuros are increasingly familiar to the Japanese people.
Awed and silent adoration has given place to popular
applause. Ho has emerged from the seclusion of the
Imperial Palace, if not to mix with the populace, at any
rate to be seen and heard by them.
From time/

Wherever the Emperor goes he is enthusiastically
acclaimed. For hours before the Royal train is due his

Peasants are as eager as officials to get a glimpse

WHERE THE ATOM BOMP HAD FAILEN
I havo been one of the onlookers during a visit the

Sir:
By the "Notice of Provisional Designation", No. G O46, dated
September 3, 1947, I was advised, in the name of the Prime Minister
that, under the provision of Paragraph 1 of Article 7-2 of the Imperial
Ordinance No. 1, of Januery 4, 1947, I was provisionally designated as
a person to be "purged". The reason specifically given is that I.
"was in the position of Ambessador
Plenipotentiary in Germany during the
period between July 7, 1937, and
September 2, 1945."
On September 30, I presented a petition for reexemination of
my cese. But the petition was not accepted and I am now definitely
designated es a "purged". Furthermore, I am made to understend, by
competent authorities of the Central Liaieon Office, that my case
belonge to a category which is commonly called, "Mandatory Cases",
by routine officiels concerned, and that persons thue designated,
are to be automaticelly end summarily excluded from public positions.
The explanation given is that "Ambassadors to Germany and Italy"
being en item specifically enumerated in Paragraph 1 of "The Criteria
for Examination and Decieion of Paragraph G Cases", the "purge" desig-
nation against me is willy-nilly final and no recourse to further
examination is to be permitted.
The "purge" is en extremely severe measure of suspending an
important part of a man's civic rights for an indefinite period.
Under the Japanese Constitution, both new and old, it could only be
enforced by a law duly legislated by the Diet. The only case in which
such a measure can be enforced by the Imperial Ordinance is when the
said ordinance is strictly in eccord with the SCAP directive based
upon the Potsdam Declaration. The Imperial Ordinance No. 1, of
July 4, 1947, which was invoked against me is an ordinance issued by
the Japanese Government for the enforcement of en order given to them
by SCAP
CONFIDENTIAL

=== Page 259 === (confidence 0.99)
Enclosure No. 2 to
Tokyo's Despatch No. 46,
dated January 21, 1948.
-2 -
CONFIDENTIAL
by SCAP in GHQ Directive of January 4, 1946 (APO 500 AG91.1.GS).
The Ordinance, thsrefo, should be looked upon as a detailed regula-
tion for enforcement of the original GHQ Directive. Such being its
nature, it should be indisputably assumed that the Ordinance must
never be allowed to overstep the boundary or stretch the objective
set by the SCAP Order in question.
From this viewpoint, let us examine the aforesaid GHQ Directive
of January 4, 1946. First we find that Paragraph 1, quotes a passage
of the Potsdam Declaration which reads in part as follows;
"There must be eliminated for all time the
authority and influence of those who deceived
and misled the people in Japan into embark-
ing on world conquest .......".
The fundamental objective of the GHQ Directive is thus clearly
defined.
Second, the seme Directive orders in its Paragraph 2, thet the
Japanese Government must remove and exclude from public and govern-
mental positions all persons who fall under the following categories:
a. Active exponents of militaristic nation-

And Appendix A of the Directive which is provided in its Paragraph 9

Now let us first consider which one of those basic provisions my
case should fall under.
Among the items enumerated, a.b.c. in Paragraph 2 of the Directive,
thorough investigation will show thet I had nothing to do with political

In this connection, it must be first taken into consideration
that the greet majority of Japanese Ambassadors are career diplomate.
While many of their American Colleagues are political appointees,
Japenese Ambassadors are usually men promoted to their positions

Ministers of State, their political significance in the Goverument

political appointees generally change when the Cabinei cimnges, but
Ambassadors usually stay on. They are under the discipline and control

Everyone knows that the variations in international relations
cannot be judged solely from the ideological viewpoint. As an American
writer recently pointed out:
"During the Thirty Years War, in an age, where chief
ideological conflict was religtous, Catholic France went
to the aid of Sweden and the German Protestants in their
conflict with Catholic Austria..... In more recent times,
Tsarist kuesie has been allied with Republican France,
democratic Britain, oligarchic Japan, democratic America,
democratic Britain with Communistic Russia and Communistic
Russie with Nazi Germany. National interests make strange
bed-fellow; in the face of a threat to the balance of power,
nations will make alliances with ideological devils".
(Ideology or Balance of Power? by William G. Carlton, The
Yale Review, Summer, 1947. p.p. 592-3).
So long as the diplomatic relations among nations are such com-
plicated affairs, it must be extremely difficult to judge the personal
ideology of a diplomat simply by the country to which he is accredited.
For instance, it must be illogical to conclude thet any American
Ambassador is a comunist only because he was stationed in the U.S.S.R.
and endeavored to maintain and develoo friendly relations between his
country and Russia.
After considering all these points, it must be fair to presume
that the cases against "Ambassadorsto Germany or Italy", in the appli-
cation of Paragraph G, should be construed as prima-facie cases, and
those who are provisionally designated should be allawed to defend
their individual cases. In regard to this point, it must be duly noted
that the "criteria" provides in its first paragraph as follows:
"Whether a person will fall under
paregraph G titled, "Additional Mili-
tarists and ultra-nationalists" will
be determined by inquiry into his past
records. Hovever, general Criteria
for such decision shall be as follows".

of the provision is not applicable to the case of an "Ambassador to
Germany". To sey the least, it is strongly doubtful whether such inter-
pretetion on the part of Japanese Authorities concerned are truly and
exectly in accord with the letter and spirit of the original Directive,
and for thet matter, with any innate sense of justico.

On October 25th, 199, while still at my post in Belgium, I
was appointed as Ambassador to Germany. Prior to this date of
appointment, when approached from Tokyo on the subject of this
Portfolio, I twice refused by cablegram but my objections were over-
ruled and I was finally obliged to accept by the persistent request
of the Minister of Foreign Affairs. All the circumstances which
brought about my assignment to Berlin, must still remain both in
the memory of Foreign Office officials concerned at the time and in
the records kept in the files of the Gaimusho. It was at the time
when the Abe Cabinet was just organized after the resignation of the
Hiranuma Cabinet. This change of Cabinets was generally attributed
to the political repercussion of the Germano-Sovietic Non-Aggression
Pact which Germany entered into without any previous intimation to
Japan in spite of a very close relationship which then existed between
this country end Germany. It can be easily understood that the
diplomatic relation with Germany in those days was not eo amicable
as it had been hitherto. The early part of my Ambassadorship in
Berlin was a period which can hardly be called active or exciting.
Cur relations with Germany then having much cooled off, my principal
duty was to see to it that this propensity of estrangement between
the two countries should not go to an unnecessary extreme. Little
or no activity on my part was necessary. But in May of the next year,
Germany started the invasion of Belgium and the Netherlands and
completed the Military occupsticn of those two countries in a short
space of time. Immediately thereafter, the German army defeated the
combined forces of Great Britain and France and entered the capital
of the French Republic in June. It is superflous to mention that
this violent change in the military situation caused a tremendous
reaction in every direction in the diplomatic relationship of the
world.
In the case of Japan, a certain group who persistently meintained
the necessity of closer ccoperation with the Axis powers suddenly re-
gained their influence and started a powerful compaign for their cause.
Secondly, even those who did not share such a viewpoint became exceed-
ingly concerned about our rights and interests in French Indo-China and
the Netherlands East Indies, these colonies having lost their Mother
Countries in Europe under the military occupation of their enemy. Under
such circumstances, we hed much to deal with Germany concerning the
protection of our interests in those regions, especially because our
government had not established any diplomatic relations with the so-
called refugee governments of Frence or the Netherlands. However, in
spite of the strong campaign of pro-axis elements in Japan, the policy
of the Japanese Government then in power, remained practically the
same and no such idca as to strengthen our relation with Germany into
a military alliance was entertained in any responsible quarter yet. The
attitude of non-committal which was hitherto maintaimed was continued
without any variation and manifestation of our policy towards Germany
always confined iteelf to the vague desire of unspecified cooperation.
The instruction given to Ambaseador Naotake Sato, Special Envoy to
Italy, who visited Berlin just about this time, clearly demonstrated
the outline of the policy of Tokyo in those days. Accordingly my
activities

activities as Ambasmador to Germany was also kept within the boundary
of this general policy of non-commitment.
However, just before the departure of Ambassador Sato from
Berlin, the second Konoe Cabinet was organized and Mr. Yosuke Matsuoka
assumed the Portfolio of Minister of Foreign Affairs. Thereupon, through
press despatches and other channels of publicity, strong clamours began
to be heard from Japan about "a great reorientation of foreign policy"
or about "reinforcement of friendship with the Axis Powers". Apparently
encouraged by such demonstrations, the German Foreign Minister repeatedly
asked me what would be the policy of the new Cabinet towards Japanese-
German cooperation. This repeated questioning necessitated my inquiries
to the new Foreign Minister on several occasions as to his (the Foreign
Minister's) future policy toward the country to which I was accredited,
and at the same time expressing my views personally of the policy Japan
should take in the prevailing world situation. My opinion was prin-
cipally based on three points:
1. The landing of German forces on the British Isles,
which was held imminent in certain quarters in
Japan, is an operation, which if successful, would
be so in one chance to a thousand, and even if it
should succeed and attain its objective, it would
certainly entail the struggle for the final
supremacy between the United States and Germany.
In such eventuality, the position of Japen placed
between the two contestants would certainly become
important and advantageous.
2. If the Japanese Government precipitates the decisi-
on of concluding a military alliance with Germany
and Italy without first exhausting every possible
means of reestablisning the friendly relations
with the USA, it will be hardly possible to attain
an unqualified approval of our public opinion and
the united support of the Japanese people behind it.
3. Japan and the United Stetes being the only principal
powers left out of the uropeen war, it should be
taken as a joint responsibility of the two countries
to prevent the disaster from spreading to the Pacific
and to prepare, if possible for the common effort of
bringing the uropean conflict to the earliest poa-
sible termination.
The Foreign Minister however, failed to enswer any of my inquiries
or to comment at all on my personal presentations. On the contrary,
the Germen side without any preliminary notification to me, sent
Mr. Stahmer over my head as a Special Envoy to Japan. My first intim-
ation of this mission I had when he called to take leave of me immedi-
ately before his departure. On this occasion I asked him if his going

-A-5

Mr. Katayama, who had absented himself from the
Social Democratic Convention in order to attend the
luncheon, stated that Japanese newspapers were crediting
the leftists in the Social Democratic Party with the
preponderence of power. He expressed certainty that
most of the strength lies with the rightists of the party.
C
He stated he would advocate abiding by the four-party
S

A
Peoples' Cooperative, and Liberal Parties, even though

the possibility that if too strong a stand were taken by

might be upset.

The major reason for leftist desire for abrogation
of the four-party agreement, according to Mr. Katayama,
was the desire on the part of the leftists to discontinue
interest on war bonds and to place a second tax on assets
and property. He felt that the leftists will give in on
the property tax, but will be adamant on the question of
discontinuance of interest on war bonds. One argument
advanced against such discontinuance, Mr. Katayama said,
is that war bonds are no longer in possession of the
people but are in banks, so that cancellation of interest
payments would affect the ability of the banks to pay
interest on other deposits. However, the leftists main-
tain that the money which could be saved by cancellation
of interest could be used for other purposes which now
have to be financed by taxes on the masses.
As the Department is aware, on January 19 (two
days after the luncheon) the Social Democratic Party,
by a vote of three hundred sixty-six to three hundred
forty-five, abrogated the four-party agreement. This
decision would appear to indicate that the leftists had
greater power in the Social Democratic Party than
Mr. Katayama had expected and arouses speculation as to
whether abrogation of the agreement may eventually lead
to collapse of the Katayama Cabinet. However, the
re-election of Mr. Katayama as Chairman of thé Central
Executive Committee and the election of Mr. ASANUMA
Inajiro as the Party's Chief Secretary implies that the
rightists still have majority strength from an administra-
tive point of view and so may be able to work out new
agreements with the People's Cooperative Party and the
Democratic Party. The strength of the rightists has
been further evidenced at the meeting of the Central
Executive Committee on January 21, at which twenty-nine
members of the committee were chosen, leaving one to be
determined later. of these, seventeen were members of
the right wing and twelve of the left. Five copies of a
list of these members, published in the Nippon Times of
January 22, are enclosed.
In discussing labor unions, Mr. Katayama said that
government workers are constantly demanding increases in
wages. He feels that workers apparently consider that
the only objective of unions is to obtain wage increases.
He inguired about the right of government workers in
the United States to strike, and when told of the non-
strike agreement signed by this class of workers, indi-
cated that only certain categories of Japanese government
workers were prohibited from striking (article no. 38
of the Labor Relations Adjustment Law). When queried
on the activities of the Communists in unions, he stated
that communists are most active in transportation and
communication unions.
When asked whether the Social Democratic members
of the Cabinet would be bound by a platform that would
be decided upon at the current Social Democratic Party
Convention

-3-
Convention, he indicated that ministers in the Cabinet
from the party would not be completely bound by the
platform, but must strive to put it into effect. He
said that the Social Democratlc Cabinet members must
necessarily take a practical point of view, otherwise,
in a coalition cabinet such as the present one the
cebinet would be unable to function.
In answer to a question as to whether the four-
party agreement barred leftist Social Democrats from
the Cabinet, Mr. Katayama said that the agreement did
not specifically include such a provision. However, he
stated that leftists were not made members of the Cabinet
because such inclusion would interfere with cooperation
with other parties.
Following a discussion of the mechanics of voting
in the United States, for example, whether the names of
candidates are always written in on ballots, Mr. Katayama
said the next session of the Diet would consider legis-
lation designed to prevent buying votes. He pointed out
that payment for votes is unfortunately customary in the
Far East. He emphasized that only by overcoming this
great difficulty could new leaders emerge as representa-
tives of the people.
Mr. Katayama, in describing difficulties facing the
Cabinet, emphasized economic problems. He stressed that,
in the next year, more strenous efforts must be made to
fight inflation, to place finances on a sound basis, to
streamline the government by efficiency of administration
and by reduction of the number of employees, and to
achieve stabilization of wages and prices. His admini-
strative address given five days later to the Second
session of the Diet was largely devoted to the urgency
of the economic situation and the intentions of the
government to devise means of improving it. Copies of
the address together with a summary are being forwarded
by despatch No. 52, January 23.
