Lir. Bevin (Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs):
". . . One other matter I must mention in passing is
Japan. There is a conflict again because it is desired
by the Soviet that we should refer the Peace Treaty to
the Council of Foroign inisters; not a very encouraging
prospect. Really, it is very difficult to agree to it.
Here are Australia, New Zealand, India, Pakistan, Burma
and the letherlands, who were all in the Japanese War
from the very day of Pearl Harbour, and while I am ready
to admit that the maintenance of great Russian armies in
the Maritime Provinces probably had an effect before they
came into the war, the actual time that Russia was in the
Japanese War was but a few days. Yot I am asked to agree
that they should take & predominant position over the
Allies who fought in the Japanese War all the way through.
Really, we cannot expect people to accept that. What we
propose is that tho 13 or 14 countries which were involved

(COPY)
UNITED STATES POLITICAL ADVISER
FOR JAPAN
MEMORANDUM OF CONVERSATION
SUBJECTS:
United States Announcement Concerning Aid to Japan for
achieving self-support; Public Reaction to Prime Min-
ister's Administrative Address; Need for New Political
Party; Influential Position of People's Cooperative
Party; Arrest of Diet Member; Impossibility of Merger
Between Liberals and Democrats; Japanese National Attend-
ing Meetin of Provisional Frequency Board; Personnel of
Communications Ministry; Comments on Communication
Workers' Union and Central Labor Relations Committee;
Cabinet Dissatisfaction with Central Liaison Office;
Need for Amending Labor Adjustment Law.
PARTICIPANTS:
MIKI Takeo, Minister of Communications;
SUZUKI Kyoichi, Vice Minister of Communications;
MATSUMOTO Takizo, Parliamentary Vice Minister for
Foreign Affairs;
W. Henry LAWREnCE, Jr., Second Secretary of Mission;
Rolland H. BUSHNER, Third Secretary of Mission.
PLACE:
Dinner iven at the residence of Foreign Service
Officers Lawrence and Bushner, Tokyo, January 29,
1948。
Sunmary. Minister Hiki stated that the announcement made by the
United States member to the Far Eastern Comission concerning aid to
Japan for achieving self-support had been received with enthusiasm by
the Cabinet and that the latter is now considering a five-year plan of
rehabilitation. He said that the Prime Minister's administrative
address was considered disappointing by most people.
Minister hiki asserted there is urgent need for a political party
with a platfonm suitable to the present times. Doth the Minister and
Hr. Matsumoto indicated that they are convineed that the People's
Cooperative Party occupies an influential position and that the
rightists of the Social Democratic Party are more closely allied in
aims with this party and the Demoeratic Party than with the left-wing
of the Social Democratic Party.
Ar. Matsumoto stated that the People's Cooperative Party had at
first sided with the Liberal Party in disagreeing as to the procedure
adopted to bring about the arrest of Mr. Hara, a Liberal Diet Member,
who is alleged to be involved in a hoarded goods scandal. Mr. Matsumoto
is convinced that there is no possibility of a merger of the Liberal and
Democratic Parties at the present time because of personal antagonism
between
CONFIDENTIAL

=== Page 291 === (confidence 0.99)
CONFIDENTIAL (For Department Use Only)
Encl. to
Tokyo's 85,
February 11, 1948.
-2-
between the leaders of the two parties.
Minister Miki described attendance of a Japanese national at
meetings of the Provisional Frequency Board in Geneva as a forward
step for Japan. Mr. Suzuki declared the Ministry is authorized
415,000 positions, but only 5,000 of these are unfilied. However,
it has 100,000 more employees than before the war, which he defended
on the grounds of increased needs due to lack of equipment plus require-
ments for maintenance of old and decrepit equipment.
Hinister Miki said that the Communists are active in the Communica-
tion Workers' Union and are members of the Central Labor Relations Com-
mittee. He mentioned the difficulty of getting employers to serve on
the Committee and the dissatisfaction of the Cabinet with the Committee
for such actions as approving the demand of electrical workers for an
average monthly wage of 5,860 yen and a sliding scale of cost of living
wage increases. Minister Miki believes the Labor Adjustment Law should
be amended to define a strike. End of Summary.
I. Cabinet Reaction to United States
Announcement Concerning Aid
to Japan
Minister MIKI stated that the announcenent made by Major General
Frank R. McCoy, American Representative to the Far Eastern Commission,
regarding the extension of aid to help make Japan self-supporting, had
been received with great enthusiasm by the Cabinet. He believes that
the fortuitous appearance of the statement in the press in Japan on the
same day as the publieation of the Prime Minister's Administrative
Address has given encouragement that the goals outlined by the Prime
Minister will be achieved. The Cabinet has under consideration at this
time a plan for economic rehabilitation which involves a fund of two
billion dollars over a peried of five years. The plan, however, has
not as yet been submitted to General lieadquarters.
Hinister Miki said that members of the Cabinet and other people
with whom he has come into contact are gratified at the confidence in
Japan which must be felt in America in order to permit such an announce-
ment to be made to the Far Eastern Commission, particularly as Japan has
so recently been an enemy country. Minister iki feels that despite
opposition on the part of certain members of the Far Eastern Commission,
the United States vill find a means of carryin out its announced plan.
Hinister Miki mentioned China and the Philippines as undoubtedly opposed
to the reconstruction of Japan on the scale advocated by the United
States; he declared that the Cabinet interprets the announcement as
indicating a trend in the United States toward including Japan within
the framework of the Marshall Plan, with Japan filling a position in
the Far East similar to that of Western Germany in Western Europe.
II. Public Reaction to the Prime Minister's Address
In referring to the Prime Minister's Administrative Address before
the Second Session of the Diet (this Mission's despatch No. 52, of
January 23, 1948), Minister Miki said that it was well received by
thoughtful intelligent people, but was considered disappointing by
many members of the Diet and by the people at large. He pointed out
that the public had placed great hope in the Katayama Cabinet when it
came into power, but considers its achievements to date small. As a
result, the popularity of the Cabinet is at a low ebb.
III. Need
CONFIDENTIAL

=== Page 292 === (confidence 0.99)
CONFIDENTIAL (For Department Use Only)
Encl. to
Tokyo's 85,
February 11, 1948.
-3-
III. Need for New Political Party
In discussing the present political situation, Minister Miki
agreed that all political parties are in ferment, being uncertain as
to their aims and policies. Members, he asserted, are selfish in
placing parties and individuals above the country as a whole. Min-
ister Miki stressed the urgent need for a political party with a plat-
form taking into consideration what is proper for Japan at this parti-
cular time in its history. He cited the impracticality of the Liberals
in advocating a "laissez-faire" economy and the Social Democrats in
advocatins socialism. He described the Democratic Party's espousal of
"revised capitalism" as enthusiasm for a hollow phrase and an example
of an attempt to reach a popular compromise ideology. He implied that
Japanese politicians are not motivated by any strong conviction as to
basic policies and hence find it easy to shift in practically any
direction, depending upon the most expedient means of extending power
by forming the most effective vote-getting combination.
IV. Influential Position of People's Cooperative Party
Eoth Minister Miki and ir. Matsumoto appeared convinced that the
People's Cooperative Party, of which they are both members, occupies
an influential position. They indicated that the importance of their
Party is evidenced by the endeavors of the major parties to enlist its
support. In this connection, Mr. Matsumoto said that he thought it
would be a good thin for Japan should there be a split anong the
Social Democrats. He asserted that the aims of rightists in the Social
Democratic Party are much more closely allied with those of the Demo-
cratic Party and the People's Cooperative Party than with those of the
left-wing Social Democratic Party.
V. Arrest of Diet Member
Mr. Matsumoto said that the Government Section of this Headquarters
expressed surprise that the People's Cooperative Party had sided with
the Liberals on the question of the Prime Minister's request for per-
mission to effect the arrest of HARA Susumu, Liberal Party Diet Member,
who is allegedly involved in a hoarded oods scandal. ir. Matsumoto
stated that he had pointed out to Government Section that the People's
Cooperative Party had not sided with the Liberals in an effort to
protect ir. Hara, but because the Party feels that the procedure used
in seeking his arrest was incorrect. The original position of the
People's Cooperative Party was that the request for arrest should have
come from the Attorney-General rather than from the Prime Minister.
To a man, Mr. Matsumoto said, the People's Cooperative Party would
have voted for the arrest of Mr. Hara, because they are convinced of
his guilt. The People's Cooperative Party later reversed its stand
on procedure and voted with members of the Social Democratic Party
and the Democratic Party for approvin: the Prime Minister's request.
The resignation of Mr. Hara and acceptance thereof by the House of
Representatives on January 30 made it unnecessary to arrest him in his
status of Diet member.
VI. Impossibility of Merger of Democratic and
Liberal Parties
Mr. Matsumoto appeared convinced that there is no possibility of
a merger between the Liberal and Democratic Parties at the present
time because of the deep personal antagonism which exists between
Dr. ASHIDA Hitoshi, President of the Democratic Party, and Mr. YOSHIDA
Shigeru,
CONFIDENTIAL

=== Page 293 === (confidence 0.99)
CONFIDENTIAL (For Department Use Only)
Encl. to
Tokyo's 85,
February 11, 1948.
-4-
Shigeru, President of the Liberal Party. He said that the same
personal antagonism exists between Dr. Ashida and Mr. SHIDEHARA
Kijuro, who has recently split from the Democratic Party. On the
other hand, according to Mr. Matsumoto, Mr. Yoshida and
Mr. Shidehara are referred to as the "Siamese twins" of Japanese
politics.
VIl. Japanese National at Meetings of Provisional
Frequency Board
Mr. SUZUKI said that the Ministry of Communications had been
given free rein in the selection of a Japanese national to accom-
pany a representative of the Supreme Commander for the Allied
Powers in the capacity of technical adviser to the meetings of the
Provisional Frequency Board in Geneva (this Mission's despatch
No. 71 of February 2, 1948). Mr. HASE Shinichi, the Japanese
national designated, was selected for four reasons: (1) his tech-
nical knowledge; (2) the fact that he had been working in this
field since before the war and has continued since the war; (3)
because his rank is high enough to enable him to gain acceptance
of his ideas upon his return to Japan; and (4) because he speaks
English.
Minister Miki feels that the attendance of a Japanese national
at meetings of the Provisional Frequency Board is a forward step
for Japan, but expressed disappointment at the censorship of the
news of Mr. Hase's departure. He mentioned that photographs had
been taken and news articles written, but that only a small notice
of the departure was pennitted by censors to appear in the press.
He agreed, however, that a lar e amount of publicity might have
arousei antagonism on the part of those countries who object to
Japanese leaving Japan until after the signing of a Peace Treaty.
VIII.
Personnel Strength of Communications
Ministry
Mr. Suzulki declared that the Ministry of Communications is
authorized to employ 415,000 employees, but that only 5,000 of
these positions are unfilled. Therefore, the Ministry of Com-
munications is facing considerable difficulty, as contrasted with
other governmental agencies having a larger proportion of unfilled
positions, in preparing for the mandatory cut in the number of
sovernment employees, which has been deseribed in this Mission's
despatch No. 78 of February 7, 1948, recording a conversation with
officials of the Ministry of Labor.
(However, while most government agencies will be required to
cut twenty-five per cent of the 1947 fiscal year budget personnel,
the number of workers in certain agencies, including the Communica-
tions Ministry, will not be arbitrarily reduced, but only after a
consideration of the number of individuals essential for the proper
functioning of the Ministry. Copy of an article translated from
the Nihon Keizai of February 1, 1948 regarding the government's
decision to reduce personnel is enclosed.)
The number of authorized positions in the Ministry is approx-
imately 100,000 above the number of people employed prior to the
war. Hr. Suzuki defended the need for this additional number on
the ground that people had to be used instead of mechanical
equipment
CONFIDENTIAL

=== Page 294 === (confidence 0.99)
CONFIBENTIAL (For Department Use Only)
Encl. to
Tokyo's 85,
February 11, 1948.
-5-
equipment because of the insafficiency of such equipment, and on the
ground that much of the equipment is so old and decrepit that it
requires large maint enance crews. As an example, he estimated that
the Ministry had 80.Oo0 bicycles before the war, but even though it
now has a priority second only to export products, the Ministry has
only 60,000 bicycles.
IX. Communi sts in Communications Workers! Union
Minister Miki said that the comnunists were active in the Com-
munications Workers! Union (Zenkoku Teishin Jugyoin Kumiai), citing
the piling up of mail at Christmas time as one of the instances of
sabotage instigated by the comunists. When asked if he had ever seen
orders in writing of the communist party concerning sabotage, he stated
that in so far as he knows, orders are passed by word of mouth.
X. Central Labor Relations Committee
In discussin the Central Labor Relations Committee, Mr. Miki
expressed conviction that there are communists among the labor repre-
sentatives who sit on the committee. He estimated that ordinarily
two out of three members of the commission are menbers of the communist
party. According to Minister Miki, the Jhairman of the Central Labor
Relations Conmittee has reat difficulty in finding employers who will
serve on the commission because of the loud and violent tactics of the
communists (many of whom sit in the audience) and the fact that no
employer wishes to antagonize labor. He indicated dissatisfaction in
the Cabinet with the Central Labor Relations Committee. As an example
of the reason for such dissatisfaction, he described the demand of the
electrical workers for an average monthly wage of 5,860 yen and a
sliding seale of inerease for the future, both of which had been
approved by the Jentral Labor Relations Commiutee and presented to the
Cabinet on January 29. The decision of the conmittee to allow a
sliding wage index for electrical workers has been previously described
by ir. TSURu Shigeto, Deputy Director of the Economic Stabilization
Board, as one of the indications that inflation may get out of hand
and lead to a collapse of the entire Japanese economy (this Mission's
despatch No. 1486 of December 30, 1947, reporting a conversation with
.P. Tsuru).
XI. Need for Amendin Labor Adjustment Law
Minister Miki was of the definite opinion that the Labor Adjust-
ment Law must be amended specifically to define a strike. At present,
the definition is so vague, he claims, that no one among the Ministers
wishes to take the risk of discharging persons for disciplinary purposes
in circunstanees which even ranotely reseable a strike because of the
danger that the situation might later be designated as a strike. Such
an event would obviously place any Minister so deciding in a disadvan-
tageous position politically and also would make him liable to a lawsuit.

Article from Nihon Keizai, February 1, 1948
(Translation)
GOVERNMENT RELEASES ADJUSTMENT PLAN
The Government, at a recent Cabinet meeting, decided to make a
25 percent horizontal reduction in the number of budget personnel in
consideration of the expected administrative readjustment, which is a
necessary condition for the compilation of the 1948 fiscal year budget
estimates. Since then, the Government has been working on a definite
plan. It informally decided upon the plan at a special cabinet meet-
ing held on 27 January and published it yesterday.
According to this new plan, in the general and special accounts
25 percent of the 1947 fiscal year budget personnel, namely 10l,000
persons, will be affected by the coming readjustment. However, the
number of persons actually affected will be 23,o00. The major govern-
ment offices expected to be readjusted are the Ministries of Foreign
Affairs, former Home Affairs, Justice, Education, Welfare, Commerce-
Industry, and Transportation (only in the general account). In con-
formity with this plan, these ministries will present their concrete
readjustment plans respectively to the Cabinet by 15 February, and the
final plan will be decided by the Cabinet by the end of February.
Concerning outdoor employees working in the Transportation Ministry,
Communications Ministry, the three bureaus of the Finance linistry
(Monopoly hureau, Printing Bureau, and Mint), Comaerce-Industry Ministry
(production of alcohol), and the Agriculture-Forestry Ministry (forest
administration alone), another plan will be made on the basis of calculated
efficiency and the number of persons needed. This will be discussed by
the ministries concerned.
fhose who are dismissed will be employed as temporary employees
until the end of July, and tlose who retire fron office at once will be
paid salaries from their retirement date to the end of July. In this
respect, the Finance hinistry will take proper steps in the budget to
raise funds for retirement allowances.
The afore-mentioned plan aims at only bemporary adainistrative re-
adjustaent and reorganization of overnrent offices necessary for the
compilation of the next fiscal budget. The fundamental reform of the
administrative organization will be taken up by the Administrative
Organization Refonn Committee to be established in the Jabinet. The
organization of the comittee will be decided at the next cabinet.meet-
ing, and the committee will begin functioning in February. This admin-
istrative readjustment plan is based upon the data as of 1 January.
Therefore, in case that govern ent offices are newly established, they
will be able to employ necessary personmel irrespecbive of this basis.
Government to Be Reorganized by Remainin Eaployees
The Goverament's announcement: In view of the change of admin-
istrative affairs and the complication of the government organization
after the surrender, the Government will execute the readjustment of
administrative affairs and the simplification of the overnment organ-
ization according to the followin: plan in order to secure maximum
administrative efficioncy and to promote sound development of general
enterprises.
(1) Keeping
CONFIDENTIAL

=== Page 296 === (confidence 0.99)
CONFIDENTIAL (For Department Use Only)
Encl. to
Tokyo's 85,
Febmuary 11, 1948.
-7-
(1) Keeping pace with the change in the situation after the
surrender, the Government will abolish unnecessary and nonvital
administrative offices and rationalize the administrative organiza-
tion by re-examining administrative affairs under the jurisdiction
of each ministry=
(2) The Government will as far as possible remove duplications
among departments or boards, secure unity in administrative affairs,
and realize clarification of responsibility.
(3) In conformity with the principle of local autonomy, powers
of the Central Government will be transferred to local self-governments
to the reatest possible extent. At the same time, existing local
agencies of the Central Government will undergo a thorough readjustment
and will be confined with local bodies as much as possible.
(4) In order to reduce personnel in conformity with the preceding
items and to realize the principle of maximum efficiency with a minimum
number, the ministries and offices will reduce their staffs, both
budgetary and organizational, with 25 percent of the budget personnel
as of 1 Jan 49 as a general standard. As for government enterprises
such as railways and communications, the degree of reduction will be
separately decided on the basis of economy and efficiency. The minis-
tries and offices will reorganize their structures with their remaining
staffs.
(5) The measure under the preceding item will not be applied to
policemen, firemen, public procurators, judiciary officials, and school
teachers.
(6) Officials who will be dismissed under the preceding items
will be retained as extras until the end of July. During this period,
however, actual dismissals will gradually be realized, while filling of
new vacancies and reassignment will be effected with these to-be-discharged
officials. If necessary, they may be employed in other offices as extras.
(7) The ministries and offices will formulate their respective
plans for reorganization and personnel reduction and will submit them
to the Cabinet before 15 February.
(8) A special committee will be set up within the Cabinet to study
fundamental reform of the administrative strueture.
Remarks: (1) Until a reorganization plan in confonmity with the
precedin itens is finally decided, the measures for preventing in-
creased strengths of government staffs and for checking the filling of
vacancies will have continued effect: (2) Public corporations and other
organizations acting for the Government, personnel expenses of which
are paid from the National Treasury, will be dealt with under the
preceding items.

Parties in Japan
The resignation of the Government
headed by Mr. TETSU KATAyAmA derives
from the present unstable condition of
Japanese party politics. His assumption
of office last May was notable on two
grounds. He was the first Socialist Prime
Minister of Japan, and he was the first
Prime Minister to be elected by the
House of Representatives under the new
constitution. From the start his position
was inherently weak. His own party, the
Social Democrats, though the largest
group in the House, number only 143;
the right-wing opposition, who call them-
selves " Liberals," hold 135 seats. The
balance of power is held by the "Demo-
crats," whose political opinions are on
the whole conservative. This last group
claimed an equal number of posts in the
Cabinet as the price of entering a coali-
tion with the Social Democrats, and MR.
KatAyamA was obliged to drive a very
mixed team. It is remarkable that he
managed to hold them together so long,
for he is no orator, has little capacity for
inspiring enthusiasm, and owes his selec-
tion as leader by his own party entirely
to his personal reputation as an upright
"middle of the road" Socialist of the
Fabian school.
In less difficult circumstances Mr.
KaTaYAmA might have retained power
even longer, but he has been confronted
by a series of problems, both political and
economic, for which his left-wing sup-
porters demanded radical solutions, while
the more conservative elements of his
coalition insisted upon a cautious policy.
He was therefore obliged to fall back upon
a series of compromises which satisfied
nobody. In his efforts to enforce honestly
the economic controls relating to produc-
tion, food, finance and banking, foreign
trade, prices and wages, he encountered
the opposition of the great Zaibatsu
combines, but he persisted in his cam-
paign, and last December struck a heavy
blow against the Zaihatsu by legisla-
tion providing for the break-up of
excessive concentrations of economic
power. This measure was opposed by
the Socialists, who believed that the
great combines ought to be nationalized
rather than destroyed, as well as by
the Conservatives, and it forms one of
the principal grounds of left-wing com-
plaint against Ma. KaTayama's adminis-
tration. Nevertheless, it may exert a per-
manent salutary influence upon Japanese
economy. In the political field Mr.
KATAYAMA's principal achievements were
the decentralization and reform of the
police and judiciary, and :e introduction
of the new criminal code,"which caused a
sensation by abolishing the crime of lèse-
majesté and gave the Emperor the same
status as ordinary mortals in the eyes of
the law. Both these measures were in-
-ensely disliked by the highly conservative
'Liberai" group in the House led by
Mr. SHigeRU YoshidA, who now claims to
succeed MR. KaTaYAMA as Prime Minister.
Whether MR. YoshiDA takes office or
not depends upon the amount of support
he can obtain from the Democrats.
Their experience in the Katayama ad-
ministration appears to have strength-
ened their dislike of social and econo-
mic reform. and to have made them
more willing to consider a coalition with
MR. YosíiDA and the "Liberals." If a
Conservatve administrarion uccedt
nower it wil! he larsely due ta. the

CENTRAL MSWS AGENCI OF CHINA
Shisei Kaikan Building

February 24, 1948
Goneral of the Army Douglas MacArthur,
Supreme Command of Allied Power,
Tokyo
Your Excellency,
Though in the throes of civil strife, the Chinese people today
are showing a tremendous interest in and paying close attention to the
work the occupation authorities are doing here in Japan.
Printed matter on postwar Japan is in great demand. Hero-worshipping
people are avidly reading your biography. People are trying to learn
more about the real situation here. They are asking whether a resurgence
of militarism is possible in postwar Japan.
With a view to helping them to a better understanding of postwar
Japan, we are taking the liberty to submit to Your Excellency the follow
ing questions:
1. Is a resurgence of militarism possible in Japan, once the
occupation is ended? Is prolonged armed occupation necessary or
sufficient to prevent it? If not, what is necessary and essential?
2. What are the thorniest problems facing the occupation
authorities?
3. Has democracy come to stay in Japan? Can a proper leader-
ship for post-occupation Japan finally evolve from among the various
existing parties?
4. Doss Cosmunism have a chance to spread in Japan?
Replies - written or otherwise - to these questions will undoubtedly
go a long way towards clearing some of the misunderstandinge and allaying
some of the fears that exist among the Chinese regarding postwar Japan.
We hope and believe Your Exeellency will be gracioue enough to gratify
our wishes and give us your views. Also we must assure Your Exeellency
that we shall withhold anything "off the record" and shall present your
views as faithfully as faithfully can be.
With best regards,
/s/ James C. Y. Shen
(James C. Y. Shen)

GENERAL HEADQUARTERS
SUPREME COMMANDER FOR THE ALLIED POWERS
Diplomatic Section
Tokyo, February 27, 1948.
My dear Hr. Shen:
In response to the questions raised by you in your letter of
February 24, 1948 to General MacArthur, I am pleased, on his behalf,
to reply as follows:
QUESTION NO. 1: Is a resurgence of militarism possible in Japan,
once the Occupation is ended? Is prolonged armed occupation necessary
or sufficient to prevent it? If not, what is necessary and essential?
ANSWER: Japan has been completely disarmed; its armed forces are
complotely demobilized, military equipment has either been
destroyed or turned into scrap, arsenals and dockyards have been
or are being rapidly dismantled. The physical equipment for any
possible military force simply does not exist. By Japan's uncon-
ditional surrender the Japanese people have been taught that
militariem is a costly undertaking which defeats its owm ends and
brings suffering and disillusionment to its proponents. In my
opinion, a resurgence of militarism in Japan is physically im-
possible for generations. In consequence, it does not appear
necessary to continue indefinitely an armed occupation.
QUESTION NO. 2: What are the thorniest problems facing the occupation
authorities?
ANSWER: It appears axiomatic that Japan can not be a peace-loving
democratic nation unless, through its own efforts, guided and
assisted by the Allied nations, it is enabled to become self-
sufficient in its economy and is able to exchange goods--raw
materials and manufactured--with countries having such raw
materials and wihich are able and willing to engage in such peace-
ful exchange. So long as countries refuse to engage in a peaceful
interchange of goods with each other, so longwill the economy of
the Far East as a whole reeain out of balance. I therefore believe
that a serious and sincere effort on the part of all Allied nations
to find a common ground for negotiation of the peace is essential.
QUESTION NO. 3: Has democracy ccme to stay in Japan? Can a proper
leadership for post-occupation Japan finelly evolve from among the
various existing parties?
ANSWER:
Mr. James C. Y. Shen,
Central News Agency of China,
Tokyo.
RESTRICTED

=== Page 314 === (confidence 0.98)
Encl. No. 2 to
Tokye's 127,
February 27, 1948
RESTRICTED
-2-
ANSWER: My answer to both questions is "Yes". I do not believe
that a people who have tasted the fruits of demecracy and who
themselves are part and parcel of the demooratic process would
again willingly revert to their former slavery. Under the
watchful guidance of the Occupation, the political parties of
Japan have grown and have nurtured and practised democratie con-
cepts. Leadership is coming to the fore among the many young
men and women who have been given an opportunity to demonstrate
their capabilities. I am confident that with further encourage
ment, guidance, and understanding from all the Allies, demoeracy
in Japan is here to stay.
QUESTION NO. 4: Does Communism have a chance to spread in Japan?
ANSWER: Communism, the extreme left, is equally as bad as the
extreme right. It is a creed of desperation which feeds upon
hunger, hardship, and hopelessness. The Japanese have already
thrown cut the extreme right; given a reasonable chance to
become a self-respecting, peace-loving, democratic nation, I
am convinced that the Japanese will likewise refuse to accept
Communism as a system.
Sincerely yours,
W. J. Sebald
Chief, Diplomatic Section
and
Chairman, Allied Council for Japan

Dr. Fine is on temporary duty in Washington. He called to answer
questions concerning Japan. In the course of the conversation he expressed the
following:
CS/A
Political Problems
The recent fall of the Katayama cabinet resulted not so much
from immediate issues like SCAp's insistence on balancing the Japanese budget,
as from basic economic problems which no Japanese cabinet can solve. As a
result of these problems the Katayama cabinet gradually lost its support. Its
coalition support lasted as long as it did, not so much from strength, as from
an unwillingness on the part of others, especially the Liberal Party, to assume
responsibility for overthrowing Katayama or forming a government.
There is no major antagonism, in the minds of the Japanese
people, between the Japanese Covernment's attitude and policies and those of
SCAP. Both the representative Japanese and the educated Japanese feel that an
alignment with the US is to Japan's interest, rather then thinking of the
Japanese view, is obligated by sheer self-interest to continue to.make
political and financial investaents in Japan. The Japanese appreciate US
support and friendship. There is no evidence whatsoever that the Japanese
will stall in order to get more aid from the US. There has been some stalling
recently, as in the case of the large coal producers, whose production records
were very poor, but the evidence shows that the reason is price difficulties,
功
especially

=== Page 319 === (confidence 0.97)
CONFIDENTIAL
2
especially price instability end a desire to consume Japan's limited resources.
A major Japanese need is a clear B progrsm on the besis of which
they can plan definitely for the next few years. At present they are
overwhelmed by uncertainties.
The Economic Stabilization Board is a creature of ScaP. No head
of ESB before Wada was effective. Other personalities in the Katayama
Goverrment, with few exceptions, were incompetents and political hacks. Some
phases of administration have been much better handled under the Katayama
Government than before, for example rationing, price control and food
collections. Rice collections are now some 9o% of quota, whereas a year ago
only some 67% of quota hed been collected. This remarkable record means an
important reduction in reliance on the black market, with its coneequent
inflationary pressure.
A basic political problem is the struggle between the left and
the right. The Communists, although few in number, are prominent in the
ideological and propaganda struggle. They have a key group in the National
Congress of Industrial Unions and probably expect to gain strength in
Japanese unions generally. The basis for SCAP opposition to strikes is
simple: SC.P cannot tolerate any major disruption of the Japanese economy;
on the other hand SCAP studiously avoids interference in small strikes. The
Communists are strong cmong teachers umions. The teachers are probably the
worst off and most frustrated of all bureaucrats, and will represent first-
class recruits for Communigm until the economic situation improves. There
is some development of sound progressivism in Japan, but Japan is still in
the melting pot and the shape of the wfld is still uncertain. Much
distmust of past leadership exists. Inflation end economic distress are
prompting the strengulation of the middle class. A fundamental factor is
1
the fundomental extreme concervatism of the Japanese people.
The most important factor in deteimining whether Japen moves to

upon the need for technology.

Economic Conditions
894.50
The Japanese standard of living, always low, is now even lower.
Prices are quite unstable. Agricultural production, alweys inedequate to
feed the people, is now about normal. Industrial production is only 45% of
the 1930-34 average, or 24% of the wartime peak. To secure the 1930-34 average
standard of living for the present population would require induetrial
production at about 125% of 1930-34.
Two basic groups of factors account for the present low level.
Losses connected with the war include severance of overseas territories,
dastruction of 30% of industrial capacity in Jepan, disruption of prewar
trade patterns with the areas which Japan occupied during the war, and loss
of substantial insurance and shipping income (Merchant Marine income used to
be $loo million a year). Technological changes of importance are the decline
of silk and the decline of Japan's cotton textile industry. Before the wer
Japan hed about 12 million cotton spindles; at the end of 1947 only 1.8
million were in operation out of somewhat over 3 million still remaining.
Japan has now about enough textile capacity for her domestic needs alone.
Cotton trade during the occupation has largely been financed by
the US Commodity Credit Corporation, which has provided raw cotton for $50
million of cotton textiles for domestic Japenese consumption and to which
there was still outstanding as of the end of 1947 a $70 million obligation.
To repay this obligation is most difficult because of the problems in getting
dollars encountered by countries which would ordinarily buy Japanese textiles.
Consequently it may be necessary to sell Japanese cotton textiles in the US.
Dr. Fine recommended to SCAP by cable a week after reaching the US that such
sales be pushed. A textile mission under Dr. Jacobs of the American Cotton
Manufacturers' Association has prepared a 16-point program. It is an ingenious
scheme to sell Japanese cotton textiles for dollars without sales in the US.
The principal suggestion is sales in former Japanese markets, a project SCAP
explored when the problem first arose. The whole Far East wants to buy
Japanese products, except raw silk, but cannot get the dollars.. Other
difficulties Japan is encountering in selling textiles in Asia crise out of
antagonism to the Jepanese, economic depression, and political disruption.
The Netherlands Eest Indies have been one of the largest buyers of Japanese
cotton textiles in the post-surrender period. In return Japan has received
some metals end oil, and in the future may get some rubber.
Jepan cen get only part of its raw cotton from India. As a result
of pressure from US cotton states a formula has been developed whereby Japan
is to get her rav cotton as follows: 40% from the US, 38p from India, 2 from
Japan now
CONFIDENTIAL

=== Page 321 === (confidence 0.99)
CONFIDENTIAL
4
Japan now gets her three mejor imports from the UB, food,
fertilizer, and petroleum. Food imports depend on allocations by the
International Emergency Food Committee, to which allocations requests are
tailored for eppropriations. Food is shipped in UB bottoms, received
by the Japanese Board of Trade, stored by them under SCAP surveillance,
and distributed through Japanese ration chanmels. Since the hungry summer
of 1946, it hes been poss1ble through the exchange during the crop year of
imported wheat for domestic rice, to provide rice for city consumption
throughout the summer, when no rice comes inte the cities from the farme.
Salt is another important import. It used to come from China. It is now
possible to get it from the US, but shipping costs bring its price in
Japan up to 10 to 15 times the cost of Chinese salt.
Japanese food production is being pressed as hard as possible.
All available area is being cultivated; including former golf courses and
eir fields. But Japan is confronted with, a losing battle on food self-
sufficiency because of diminishing returns from cultivation of limited
acreage and because of population growth. Total population in Japan has
risen from 72 million at the time of surrender to 78.5 million at present
as a result of repatriation and naturel increase. It appears that the
rate of natural increase is now declining, although population statistics
are not very good.
Economic Recovery
Japen's major economic needs today are sufficient rice, textiles,
housing and coal. Even present inadequate standards can be maintained only
with considerable imports from the US; with trade patterns what they now are
these imports from the US cannot be paid for with the proceeds of exports,
and continued US aid is necessary. No recovery in Japanese production
and consumption will come about without substential and long- ange
rehabilitation of the economy.
Plans for economic recovery heve been prepered in Japan as well
as in Washington. The Economic and Scientific Section of SCiP drew up a
plan in the fell. It was approved by General MacArthur and brought to
Washington by Mr. Emerson Ross, end on it was based the Army Depertment's
request for a $l8o million rehabilitation cppropriation now before the
Bureau of the Budget. In the early steges of the preperation of the ESS
recovery plan the Japenese Covernment cooperated closely. Later the
Japanese submitted e series of plens on different recovery problems,
prepared at Dr. Fine's request by the Japanese Covernment working on its
owm. These plans cre in no sense official Japanese plans, since ESs wants
to avoid difficulties such as those resulting from press reperts about
Jepanose "demends" in connection with economic recovery.
Dr. Fine left Tokyo three weeks after General McCoy made his
st tement in the Far Eastern Commission on the US intention to foster
economie recovery in Japan. During those three weeks no instruction was
received by SCAP on asking the Japanese Government to submit en official
economic recovery

CONFIDENTIAL
5
economic recovery progrem in accordance with General McCoy's statement.
The Japanese have not lost their capacity to work, and in this
sense they renresent a good bet for the US, in fact as good a place as any
for US aid. There are no beggars in Japan. But this Japanese ability does
not assure that success will be attained in plans to make Japan self-
supporting. Such success depends on the world trade pattern and on the
intelligence of the US cid program and other complementary programs.
Present chaos in world trade is the basic difficulty.
is to the need for intervention in the administration and
control of the Japanese economy, the growing SCAP intervention arose out
of widespread Japenese incompetence and a certain amount of very able
opposition such as that offered by former Finance Minister Ishibashi. Much
of SCAP cnd ESS intervention is simply educating the Japanese, with whom
there is much discussion and cordial exchange of ideas. Dr. Fine is not
afraid SCAP is pampering or restricting the Japanese.
In administering a recovery program the Japenese should be given
the maximum latitude, but SCAP must retain the right to insist on adequate
performance. The US must determine a simple set of standards, especially
setting up specific itoms for review cnd criteria for their review. It is
a simple necessity that we gradually withdrew our intervention in the
Japenese economy. We have much Japenese good will, and this will help in
the cdministration of a self support program.

CHAPTER I. CONVOCATION AND TLECTION OF OFFICERS
Article 1. Members shall assemble in the House of Repre-
sentatives at ten o'clock on the morning of the day designated
for convocatfon by the Imperial Rescript.
Article 2.: Newly elerted members must present to the
Secretariat for verification their certificates of election.
Article '3. If vacancies exist in the offices of both
Speaker and Vice Speaker on the day of convocation, the House
shall elect the Speaker after one-third of the members are
present.
The election of the Speaker shall be conducted by secret
ballot, or by signed ballot if the Hou-e so.decides.
Article 4. If election is hy secret hallot, each member,
in response to roll-call, shall carry his ballot and wooden
name-ticket to the ballot box on the rostrum.
Secretary A shall receive the name ticket and secretary B
the ballot, and they. on hehalf of each member, shall cast the
name-ticket and ballot into the name-ticket and ballot boxes
respectively.
Article 5. When all members present have voted, the
Secretary General shall declere that the voting is closed,
after which declaration no further ballots shall be cast.
Article 6. On completion of the voting, the Secretary
General shall at once have the ecretaries count the name-
tickets and hallots cast and examine the ballots.
In case the number of  ballots cast exceeds the numher
of name-tickets, unless such excess does not affect the result
of the election, a second election shall he held.
Article 7. On completion of the examination of the ballots,
the Secretary Goneral shall report the result of the election.
Article 8. He who has received a maiority of the votes is
declared elected.
If no candidate obtains a majority of votes, a final election
shall:be held to decide between the tvo candidates who obtained
the largest number of votes; he who then receives a majority
is elected: In case, however, the two candidates in the final
election obtain an equal number of votes, the decision shall
be made by lot.

Chapter I
General Provisions
Article l - The number of members of the House of Coun-
cillors shall be two hundred and fifty (25o), to be divided
into 150 members from the prefectural constituency and 100
members from the national constituency.
Members from the prefectural constituency shall be
elected in each of the election districts. The election dis-
tricts and the number of members to be returned for each of
such districts shall be stipulated in the annex.
Members from the national constituency shall be elected
in a single constituency comprising the Metropolis, the Dis-
trict (Dā) and all the Prefectures.
Article 2 - The voting districts and the ballot-counting
districts shall conform respectively to those districts for
the election of members of the House of Representatives. .
Chapter II.
Voting Right and Eligibility
Article 3 - Any person who has the right to vote in
the election of members of the House of Representatives shall
have the same right in the election of members of the House
of Councillors.
Article 4 - Any Japanese national who is over thirty
(30) years of age shall be eligible for election of the mem-
bers of the House of Councillors.
Article 5 - Any person who has been declared incompetent
or quasi-incompetent, or who has been condemned to nenal
servitufe or confinement and whose term of punishment has
not been completed or is yet to be executed shall neither be
eligible for election nor possess the right to vote.
Article 6 - Commissioners for Overseeing the Election
of members from the national constituency, Commissioners for
Overseeing the Election of members of the Metropolitan Assembly,
Commissioners for Overseeing the Election of members of the
District and Prefectural assemblies, Commissioners for Over
seeing the Election of members of the Municipal, Town and
Village Assemblies, secretaries of the Commission for Over-
seeing the Election of Members from the national constituency,
Commission for Overseeing the Election of Members of the Met-
ropolitan Assembly, Commissions for Overseeing the Election of

Chapter IV
Voting
Article 20 - Each elector shall cast only one ballot in
the election of members from the prefectural constituency
and in that of members from the national constituency res-
pectively.
Article 21 - Voting Overseers shal1 be selected and
appointed by the Commissions for Overseeing the Election of
Members of the Municipal, Town, and Village Assemblies,
from among those who have the right to vote in the election
of members of the House of Councillors.

stituency and that of Members from the national constituency

Assemblies may appoint the Voting Overseers for the Election
of Members from the prefectural constituency concurrently
to the Voting Overseers for the election of Members from the
national constituency.
Voting overseers shall take charge of affairs pertain-
ing to election.
Article 22 - Candidates for membership may choose one
(1) person who will be a Voting Witness, from among those
registered in the electoral list of each voting district,
with his consent, and report the choice to the Voting Over-
seer not later than two days before the date of the election.
In case those reports as provided for in the preceding
paragraph (excluding those reported by candidates for member-
ship who have died or withdrawn their candidacy: the same
applies hereinafter) do not exceed ten (1o) in number, they
shall at once be Voting Witnesses, and in case they are more
than ten (10), ten (10) Voting 1tnesses shall be clected by
mutual vote from among those reported.
When the number of the Voting Witnesses provided for
in the preceding paragraph does not reach three (3) or has
decreased to less than three (3), or when the number of the
Voting Witnesses who have attended at tho polling place has
not reached three (3) by the time to open it or has decreased
to less than three (3) after it has been opened, Voting Over-
seers shall select and appoint such number of Voting wit-
nesses as makes their total number thrce (3), from among
those registered in the electoral list of the electoral
district concerned and immediately notify those who have
been selected and appointed, to witness voting.
Voting Witnessos shall not resign their offices without
proper reason.
Article 23 - Every elector shall enter by himsclf the
full name of one candidate in a ballot at a polling-place
in the election of Members from the prefectural constitu-
ency or in the election of Members from the national con-
stitueney respectively and cast it in a ballot-box.
The name of an elector shall not be entered in a ballot.
Article 24 - Denial of voting shall be decided by the
Voting Overseer, after consulting with Voting "itnesses.

THE LAW FOR THE EL CTION OF MEMBERS
OF THE HOUSE OF REPRESENTATIVES
The Election Districts
Article 1 - The members of the House of Representatives
shall be elected in each of the election districts. The
election districts and the number of members to be elected in
each district are set forth in the appendix to the present
law.
Article 2 - The voting districts shall be subject to the
limits of cities, towns and villages.
When the Commissions for Overseeing the Election of Mem-
bers of the Municipal, Town or Village Assemblies deem it
necessary, there may be established several voting districts
for one city, town or village.
In case voting districts are established according to
the preceding clause, the Commissions for Overseeing the
Election of Members of the Municipal, Town or Village Assem-
blies must immediately announce the fact.
In case any provisions of the present law are not ap-
plicable to districts established according to the second
clause of this article, special provisions may be enacted by
imperial ordinance.
Article 3 - The ballot-counting districts shall be sub-
ject to the limits of cities, towns and villages.
When the Commission for Overseeing the Election of Mem-
bers of the Metropolitan Assembly or Commissions for Over-
seeing the Election of Members of the District or Prefectural
Assemblies deem that there are special circumstances, there
may be established several ballot-counting districts for one
city or one ballot-counting district for several towns or
villages.
When the ballot-counting districts are established
according to the preceding clause, the Commission for Over-
seeing the Election of Members of the Metropolitan Assembly
or Commissions for Overseeing the Election of Members of the
District or Prefectural ssemblies must announce the fact
immediately.
In case any provisions of the present law are not ap-
plicable to ballot-counting districts established according
to the second clause of this article, special provisions may
be enacted by imperial ordinance.
Article 4 - When an alteration takes place in an election
district in consequence of a change in administrative bound-
aries, the members actually sitting for such district shall
retain their seats.
Voting Right and Eligibility
Article 5 - Any Japanese national who is over tventy
years of age shall have the right to vote.
Any Japanese national who is over twenty-five years of
age shall be eligible for election.
Article 6 - Any person who has been declared incompetent
or quasi-incompetent, or who has been condemned to penal servi-
tude or confinement and whose term of punishment has not been
completed or is yet to be executed shall neither have the
right to vote nor be eligible for election.

=== Page 431 === (confidence 0.99)

Article 7 - Deleted.

of Members of the Metropolitan Assembly, Commissioners for
Overseeing the Election of Members of the District or Prefect-
ural Assemblies, and Commissions for Overseeing the Election
of Municipal Town or Village Assemblies, Voting Overseers,
Ballot-Counting Overseers and Chairmen of Election, and
officers and officials engaged in the management of affairs
pertaining to election shall not be eligible for election
within the limits of the jurisdiction of their respective
offices.

tors, revenue officials and police officers in active service
shall not be eligible for election.

Such a demand may not be made after expiration of the

Article 15 - Upon the receipt of a notice set forth in
the preceding article, the Commission for Electing Members

A new electoral list shall be compiled whenever a

Sir:
I have the honor to enclose five copies of General
Order No. 4, March 13, 1948, issued by General Headquarters,
Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers, on the subject of
"Intelligence Targets in Japan".
The Department's attention is respectfully invited to
subparagraphs d, and e, of paragraph 6 of the enclosure,
from which it would appear that this Mission, in its
capacity as Diplomatic Jection of this Headquarters, is
precluded from exclusive exploitation of any intelligence
material and records in Japan unless a request is made
through the Translator and Interpreter Service, Document
A/MJS
Section, Tokyo, under control of the Assistant Chief of
Staff, G-2; and further, from sending any reports, publi-
cations, etc., of possible intelligence value to the De-
partment without prior clearance through the Assistant
Chief of Staff, G-2.
A literal reading and construction of General Order
No. 4 would prohibit all objective reporting on the part
of this Mission, unless the Chief of ission is prepared
to submit reports having a "possible intelligence value"
to G-2 Section for approval. On the other hand, to cont nue
reporting to the Department on subjects pertaining to th
Japanese situation might, it is believed, subject me, as
Chief of the Diplomatic Section, to possible reprimand by
the Supreme Commander.
It is not my intention to raise this question with the
Supreme Commander in view of possible misunderstanding to
which any conceivable approach on this subject might sive rise.
CONFIDENTIAL
As the

=== Page 475 === (confidence 0.98)
Tokyo's.172
March 17, 1948.
-2-
CONFIDENTIAL
(For Department Use Only)
As the Department is aware, by the integration of this
Mission into General Headquarters its freedom of operation
in the normal sense was largely lost. It is my understanding,
however, that the Department has not abandoned the principle
that its officers in any foreign country, if they are prop-
erly to carry out their functions, must be free to report
objectively concerning matters of interest to the Department.
It is my considered recommendation to the Department
that no issue be made of this question at the present time,
as to do so might perhaps destroy the pleasant and smooth
working relationships which have been established between
this Mission and the Supreme Commander and his Headquarters.
This despatch, therefore, is written primarily with a
view to apprising the Department of the difficult circum-
stances which appertain to our efforts to accomplish our
mission in Japan.
Respectfully yours,

Subject: Forwarding Memorandum of Conversation with
Former Prime Minister KATAYAMA Tetsu.
(4)
The Acting Political Adviser has the honor to enclose
894.00/3-1748
a copy of a memorandum of conversation, dated March 15,
1948, between the Acting Chief of Mission and former Prime
Minister KATAYAMA Tetsu.
Mr. Katayama gave as the reason for the resignation
of his Cabinet the desire on his part to prevent an
irreparable split within the Social Democratic Party.
This split apparently was threatened because of growing
friendly relations between certain members of the extreme
left-wing elements of his party with the Japan Communist
Party leadership, a circumstance which threatened party
unity. Mr. Katayama attributed his resignation to a
desire on his part to devote full time to re-establishing
party discipline and unity.
In discussing the progress of Communism in Western
European countries, Mr. Katayama appeared greatly relieved-
when told that the policy of the United States Government
is to resist Communism, particularly in countries where
the majority of the people are not in sympathy with
Communism. He stated that the Social Democratic Party will
never join with the Communists and cited the refusal of his
party to follow the lead of certain of its left-wing ele-
ments in joining a so-called People's Front in Japan.

MEMORANDUM OF CONVERSATION
PARTICIPANTS: Mr. Tetsu KATAYAMA
Mr. W. J. SEBALD
Former Prime Minister KATAYAMA Tetsu called at his
own request with a view to explaining the reasons for
the recent resignation of his Cabinet. Mr. Katayama
stated that general opinion is that his Cabinet resigned
because an impasse had developed within the Cabinet on
certain major policies. This, he stated, is not true.
The real reason for the Cabinet resignation was a desire
on the part of Mr. Katayama, as President of the Social
Democratic Party, to prevent an irreparable split within
the party into right-wing and left-wing factions.
Mr. Katayama indicated that the extreme left-wing
elements of his party were becoming very friendly with
the Japanese Communist Party leadership and that such
left-wing elements were insisting upon radical policies
which he felt the Social Democratic Party could not accept,
much less carry out. He said that a small faction of four
or five members, known as the Yokyoha (friendly-to-the-
Communists faction) were exercising considerable influence
over an additional twenty or so left-wing members and that
it became apparent to him that unless he devoted personal
attention to party matters, a dangerous split would occur.
For this reason he decided that his Cabinet must of
necessity resign in order to give himself freedom of action
in mending the bad schism which was in the making. Having
resigned, he now intends to devote his full time to travel-
ing throughout Japan with a view to re-establishing party
di scipline.
Mr. Katayama said that Dr. ASHIDA had been persistent
in his efforts to have him join the new cabinet in some
capacity or other, but that he has steadfastly refused
these invitations, as to do so would again force him to
give too much time to cabinet affairs. On the other hand,
he has agreed to serve as an adviser to the Foreign Office
and hopes in this way, notwithstanding his lack of experience
in foreign affairs, indirectly to throw the full weight of
his Party behind the new Cabinet.
Mr. Katayama asked me concerning the progress of Com-
munism in Western European countries and wondered whether
the proposed alliance between England, France, and the
Benelux countries would have any effect on other countries
of the world. I replied that the proposed alliance has
CONFIDENTIAL
the full

=== Page 498 === (confidence 0.99)
Encl. to
Tokyo's 170
March 17, 1948
-2-
CONFIDENTIAL
(For Department Use Only)
the full sympathy of the United States in that it indicates
a hardening on the part of Western European countries in
resisting the inroads of Communism. I further stated that
it is the policy of the United States Government to resist
Communism, and particularly in countries where the majority
of the people are not in sympathy with Communism. Mr.
Katayama expressed great relief to learn this and said that
I may rest assured that the Social Democratic Party will
never line up with Communism and that it will do its utmost
to prevent further infiltration by Communists into Japanese
labor unions, the Government, etc.
Mr. Katayama referred to Communist efforts some time
ago to draw the socialists into a so-called People's Front
in Japan, at which time the Social Democratic Party refused
to follow the lead of certain of its left-wing elements and
Communist sympathizers. He said that this policy is still
basic in his Party and that while he felt Japan's future lay
in the establishment of a social democratic country, Com-
munism must have no part in Japan.
W. J. Sebald

=== Page 506 === (confidence 0.99)
Enclosure No. 1 to Despatch No. 208
dated March 30, 1948 from the Office
of the United States Political Adviser
at Tokyo, on the subject: "Inaugura-
tion of the Democratic Liberal Party."
Declaration
e, who have the sane aspirations, get together and hereby
forn a new political party, with a view to saving our fatherland
fron distress, and to brinring hope and stability to the people
in despair anu restlessness.
At present there are many political parties in our country.
Some are ruled by biased and nirrow-minded dogmatism, hindering
rehabilitation of the nation and the national life. Others are
bound by the immediate party protits, having no courage and
strength to remove evils of the tine.
The cancer for the reconstruetion of Japan is the predomi-
nance of socialistic ideoloy and the existence of fedualistic
bureaucracy canouflaged under the cloak of socialism. These two
factors suppress the individualities of the people, prevent their
economic and cultural develcpments, make their hearts stagnant,
and enhance subservieney to power and toadyism.
We aim at the establishment of such normal economic and
social life as wil! develop the talent of each individual freely
and equally, and properly reward his or her capacity and diligence.
This is the very foundation of democracy and the condition by
which demoralization now sweeping the country is rectified. By
this alone the efficieney of industry and public administration
is recovered, a speedy rehabilitation of the Japanese economy can
be expected, and the elevation of the national life and constant
expansion of productive power can be made possible through con-
stant inerease of productive power. There can be no increase of
distribution without inerease of production. e equally respect
the position of labor and management. The construction of such a
society must depend upon creative thought, standing upon human
nature and realistic policy.
We hope that the Japanese will become an international people
in the proper sense of the term. The militaristic self-sufficient
economy in the vast must promptly be reorganized to be suitable to
peaceful conmercial econony. In an attempt to ioin the inter-
national community economically and politically, Japan must en-
force scientific and cultural activities, with full respect for
positive intelligence.
Needless to say, we realize that Japan is surrounded by in-
surmountable difficulties. We, however, cannot stay indifferent
to see poor and ambiguous politics doubling these difficulties
and leading the people to difficult situations.
We hereby establish a political party with determination to
fulfill its historic mission of rebuilding Japan as the light of
the country.

=== Page 507 === (confidence 0.99)
Enclosure No. 2 to Despatch No. 208
dated March 30, 1948 from the Office
of the United States Political Adviser
at Tokyo, on the subject: "Inaugura-
tion of the Democratic Liberal Party."
Purpose of the Formation of the
New Political Party
Folitics is the basic design for changin: the unfortunate
age brought about by the defeat of war into a bright period. The
present politics, however, are confused and unstable, with sheer
continuation of blan pages. Under such a condition, when can the
nation be rebuilt?
Today, there are two currents in our politics. Democracy
that respects the freedom and personality of an individual, and
socialisn shackled by ideology. The forner is what the mass of
people ardently desire. And yet political power which should have
been crystallized has not heen materialized. This is the greatest
reason for a confusion of the political situation which was hin-
drance to the execution of effective and pertinent policy, despite
destitution of the national life.
We have long been advocating political unity by means of a
creat unity of those havin the same purpose in view. The oppor-
tunity has now ripened, and the time has arrived for the establish-
ment of a new political party.
The new party we are proposine aims at a popular and progres-
sive character based upon national sentiment and responding to the
international situation.
Ne reject needless class struggle, strive to bring about in-
dustrial rehabilitation and stability of national life. We execute
the principle of production first at home, and expedite a speedy
and over-all opening of international trade, thereby recovering
the national fate which is now in a sad plight, and speeding to
the construetion of a country with high cultural flavor.
The situation at home and abroad no longer permits hesita-
tion. In an effort to establish a responsible political structure
by casting aside all partisan sentiment and relations in the past,
and in full conformity with the core of the new Constitution, we
are now organizing a fresh, powerful and truly national party.
It is hoped that the people havine the same purpose and ideals
will support and join this new party.

われて、時弊を取り除く勇氣と力を持たない
日本再建の癌は實に社會主義的觀念論の横行と社會主義によつて
擬裝せる封建的官僚主義の飛存であるこの二つぶ國民の個性を抑壓
しその經濟的文化的能力の發揮をさまたげ人心を沈滯せしめて、權
力に對する卑屈と事大主義とに拍車をかけている
われらは國民各自の才幹が自由に均等な機會をもつて發揮せられ
才能と勤勉が正しく報いられる正常空經濟的社命的生活の樹立を目標
とするこれこそ民主主義の根底であり滔々たる道德的額廢を克服

本經濟の速な復興が期待之れ生産力の絕えさる擴大に作つて國民生
活の向上と家庭生活のうるおいが可能となる生産の増強なくして分配

一、農水産物價格と工業製品價格との均衡をはかると共に、農林水産金融の回滑化を期する
一主食類については地力に應じて責任生産量を定め、責任量の供出後は一定條件の下に自由處分
を認める。
一、健全な新農村建設のため全農業者の協力を基本とする農民組合を育成して、科學的農法の指
導と精農運動の中核たらしめる。
一、遠洋漁業の振興と浅海内水面の草漁業の奬剛をはかり、各種漁業用資材の確保を期する
森林資源の培養のため全國前に植林を賞施すると共に林道網の整備後充をはかる。
一綜合的國土計遊を樹立し電源開發、戰災地復興災害復得、治山治水及正港測道路の整備
復興を積極的に行う。
一、海遞、鐵道及び小還送の整備調整をはかり、交通運輸の能率化を期する
財政金融
一、因民經済の實力に相感する貸貧的健全財政を堅持し、インクレーションの抑止と、通貨の安定
お期する
一、國民負落の通正と産業再建の見地より孫算通成を行い政府支拂監盜の儀格化を期し官業に
ついては極力経營の刷がをはかる。
一、所得税の基礎控除を引き上げ、且つ所得税及び法人税の稅率を輕減する
一、間所得と脱税に對してはその抽捉を後底し且つ煙草等の増産による増收をはかる
一、中央及び地方税制の綜合調監を行い地方財源の充實をはかる
一、生産復興を促進するよう生産金強の四滑をはかり、日つ復興金過金庫の後能を刷新すると共に
各種の指近を語じて時落の増強に努める。
勞働社會
一、貸金の重点を漸次生活給より能率給に移行し、勤勞所得税の累進卒を輕減する又生活必語
物資の圓滑なる入手をはかり、勤勞者の生活安定方策を推進する
一、勞資協力による勞働法規の回滑なる巡用により勞通組合の億全な發違を促し、公明なる圓題
協約の締結によつて産業半和の確立をはかる。
母性及び乳幼見の保護施策を充官する。
一、公營の住宅建設を促進すると共に、個人住宅について建築制限を殺和する
公共醫療施設を充實整備寸ると共之傷獲者遺家族戰災者引揚者貧窮者の厚生施策を
推進する
一、海外同胞の引揚を本年中に完了すべく一府の努力を拂う。

May 20, 1948
STATUS OF THE PURGES IN JAPAN
(Source: NA)
As of May 1948, approximately 95% of the various purges undertaken in
Japan have been completed, with approximately 200,00 persons removed or
excluded from public office and from key positions in the economic and
cultural life of Japan. No new categories have been added to the purge list
since last year, and present plans contemplate relaxation of the program
hereafter, rather than the addition of sny new groups. In relation to the
economic reccvery personnel needs of Japan, it is felt that the purges may
already have been carried too far.
The major goal of the purge program was to eliminate from leadership in
Japan those groups considered responsible for Japanese militaristic nationalism
and aggressive expensionism. From the beginning of the occupation the responsi
Hlity for administering the program hes been in Japanese hands, in accordance wit
6
detailed instructions from SCAF and under SCAP's general supervision.
Groups thus removed from office or barred from appointment or election to
office include over 150,000 military, neval and Gendermerie officers, 45,000
influential members of ultra-nationalistic political and patriotic societies and
agencies. In addition, the economic purge has affected about 1500 key persons in
commerce, industry, finance and agricultural and 70o in the public information
media field. Corresponding action was taken in the educational system.
20
The purges in Japan have differed in three significant respects from the
4
denazification activities in Germany. In the first place purgees in Japan have
been identified by categories rather than as indiviuels. Second, the only penalty0
imposed in the Japanese purges has been diqualification from office. Purgees,
other than war criminals, have not been subjected to imprisonment, fines, or pro-
perty confiscations. In the third place, the manner of administration of the
Japanese purges has been such that only persons in office or aspiring to office
have been affected. It is felt, however, that the coverage of persons in the
affected categories has been substantially complete, so that there is no one now
in governmental or key private positions who falls clearly within purged categories,
and that there remain relatively few affected aspirants to such offices who have
not been notified in advance of their ineligibility.
The present status of the progrem is that the national level Central Screening
Board of the Japanese Government has been reduced to a smell residual unit in the
office of the Frime Minister, and although the prefectural screening boards are still
in existence, the volume of their activities is rapidly declining.
S
There are two principal problems which remain for the future:
A
4
1. There is the prospect of en incresse in the criticism vhich has
already been voiced, as to the justice of discualifying persons for
office by categories rather then following examination of the
records and histories of individusls. For the duration of the
2
occupation this is clearly not a serious threat to the purpose of
the purge program.

=== Page 519 === (confidence 0.99)
-2 -
2. The clear need for a concerted effort towards economic recovery,
to establish a peaceful and independent nation that can play its
part in Far Eastern and World affairs without reliance on abnormal
outside help, is already generating a demand for the return to
active roles of experienced and able purgees: Fressure in this
direction may be expected to increase over the next few years and
some compromise with the principles laid down in the immediate post-
surrender phase appears indiceted during the rebuilding phase of
Japanese history which lies ahead.
This substantial completion of the purge program, should not lead to complacency
regarding the attainment of the anti-militaristic and democratizing objectives of
the occupation of Japan. The fight goes on between those elements in the Japanese
society, such as the intrenched bureaucracy, which generally escaped the purges,
and which clings substantially to old patterns of thought, and those newer elements
such as the liberal trade unions and farn groups which are being weaned away from
feudal restrictions towaris the role of potential supporters of democracy in Japan.
Our hopes for the future of Japan must rest on the mergence of a native leadership,
as free as possible from the stigme of subservience to the foreign occupying power,
if the destructive effect of the purges is to be followed by the constructive
developments which constitute our underlying objectives.

Dear Sebald:
Would you be good enough to let me know the status
of the appeal of Yoshio Osawa who was purged beoause of
the executive position he held in a Japanese film company
I make this request not so much because he is a olassmate
of mine and I personally wish him well, but beoause he
has a host of friends in the United States many of whom
are friends or aoquaintances of mine or feel themselves
free to get in touoh with me and do so with great and
inoreasing frequenoy. I want to be in a position to give
them definite information.
Osawa went to Lawrenceville School for five years
and Princeton for four years. He graduated from Prinoeton
1n 1925 and was one of the most popular members of that
olass. On returning to Japan, he worked with General
Motors until it closed up its operatione in the latter
part of the 30's. As a result, a large number of solid
oitizens and not a few important people have had continu-
ous contact with Osawa over a number of years and they
regard him as the epitome of the type of Japanese who
should come to the fore in Japan if the purposes of our
occupation are to be consolidated by action on the part
of the Japanese themselves.
Every few days I get an inguiry from someone who
has heard, not from Osawa but from a fellow Amerioan.
that he is in difficulty and who finds it incredible that
he should be purged.
All this leads me to write asking would you let me
know what the status of his cese is and whether his
personal standing has. on appeal, overcome the category
of the position he held during the wer or if not what
the case against him is in brief.
With kindest regarde.
Faithfully yours.
W. Walton Butterworth

: HMB
FROM : FMF
suct: Shangha1's 1213 of May 30th
I talked with Major King, of the Public
Information Division of the Department of
the Army, who has been assigned action on
the attached. I suggested that in their
wire to Tokyo they indicate that information
had come to their attention that Mr. Woo
would be available to go to Japan to do a
series of articles for the Shanghai Evening
Post and Mercury, that the State Department
had been consulted and heartily endorsed
the project as being in the national interest
in view of the present situation in China,
and that invitational orders be issued if
possible.
Major King explained that "invitational
orders""brings up a budgetary problem as
well as one of precedent. He explained
that at one time Secretary Royall's sugges-
tion that invitational orders be issued to
US editors had been turned down, but at
last admitted that SCAP could in his dis-
cretion overcome these difficulties and
it would be pointless to anticipate them now.
Major King promised that a wire would
go out this afternoon and that he would
telephone when the reply has been received.

FOREWORD
In this series of Current Japanese Public
Opinion Surveys, Civil Information and Iducation
Section presents brief analyses of surveys by
Japanese agencies of the attitudes of the Japa-
nese people toward significant current issues.
In some cases, discussion of these findings will
have appeared in the Japanese press. In this
series, each public opinion survey which is re
ported is evaluated from the point of view of
general reliability both of techniques and of
findings. This evaluation is intended as an in-
dication of the acceptability of the surveys as
measures of Japanese attitudes.
The analysis in this series of a survey by
a Japanese public opinion agency does not con-
stitute either an endorsement of that agency or
approval of the findings.

ATTITUDES OF TOKYO RESIDENTS TOWARD THE ASHIDA CABINET
Yoron Kagaku Kyokai, February 1948
THE SURVEY
THE PROBLEA
In February 1948, Mr. Hitoshi ASHIDA was elected Prime Minister by
the Japanese Diet. The election was by a small margin of votes after a
great deal of disagreement in both houses of the National Diet. The
opposition remained vocal and articulate even after the fornation of
the new Cabinet, and demanded the dissolution of the Diet and a general
election to reascertain the popular mandate. It was contended that
changes in popular sentiment had altered the representativeness of the
Dict.
THE SURVEY
In order to test the various claims and counterclains, the Associ-
ation for Public Opinion Science (Yoron Kagaku Kyokai) conducted a poll
of attitudes toward the newly formed ASHIDA Cabinet on 22 Fobruary 1948,
the day after the announcenent of the election of Mr. ASHIDA. It inter
viewed 5l6 persons in a carefully selected cross section of the Tolyo
population.
SUMARY OF HE FINDINGS
The seneral results of the survey indicated that public attitude
toverd the Cabinet was lukewarm, with resignation and vatchful vaiting
as the cominant tone. It was found also that a plurality of all re-
spondents favored dissolution of the Diet end the holding of new elce-
tions. That a general shift of public political sentiment had occur-
red was indi cated by the fact that the Laberals emerged as the strong-
cst single perty, a reversal of previous tendeneies in Toleyo, vhere
the Social Democratic Party had been strongest, as shown by the 1947
Diet clcctions and subsequent public opinion surveys.
RELIADILITY OF THE FIIDINGS
The general findings of this survey seem to be feirly reliable,
although the number of persons polled was too small a sample of the
population to give high reliability in the detailed breakdowms.

SIGFIFICANCE OF THE FINDINGS
This study represents the attitudes of the small but carefully
selected cross section of the population of Tokyo the day after the en-
nouncement of the appointment of Mr. ASHIDA as Prine Minister. It
seems to emonstrate that there was no popular enthusiasm for the
choice, and that uncertainty and an attitude of resignation and probably
of unconcern vere prevalent.
The findings of this Tolyo survey may be construed as indicative of
national opinion despite possible cifferenccs in political opinion be-
tween Tolgo end the rest of Japan. The small minority support accorded
the AShIDA Cabinet, as revealed by this survey, is comparable to the
minority support reported for the KATAYMa Cabinet in national surveys
conducted in the latter part of 1947 and early in 1948. Early surveys

in previous surveys. During the April 1947 elections they vere able to
predict very closely the outcome of the Diet elections in Tolyo by use
of an extremely small sample.
The present sample was based upon modem considerations of random
sanpling by area sampling design. Its relative success is indicated by
the fact that the age composition of male and female groups of the
